papers.title: CollabFlow: Recursive Self-Improvement of Agent Collaboration
papers.summary: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) lets a system improve from its own outcomes; in LLM-based multi-agent systems, Agents refine one another within a task, and outcomes improve how they collaborate across tasks. However, existing multi-agent collaboration leaves this loop open: collaboration is pre-defined at the operator level, topology-only learning keeps verbatim exchange that propagates errors, and reward maximization on a system's own outcomes concentrates on a few teams. To address these challenges, we propose CollabFlow, an RSI system of Learned Agent Collaboration: a trainable Collab-Director constructs teams of complete Agents, a frozen executor runs them, and each round's outcomes retrain the director. Within each round, the edges of a collaboration graph carry protocols of Evidence-Conditioned Communication: a receiver adopts a differing answer only when the sender's evidence is stronger by a margin, so the director learns who communicates and how. Across rounds, we further propose Collaborative Trajectory Balance (CTB), a flow-based objective that credits each team once across its construction orders and targets a reward-proportional distribution over teams, so several good teams stay in play. We also bound how far this self-generated target moves between rounds, which shrinks as records accumulate. On twelve datasets, CollabFlow outperforms all baselines and keeps improving across rounds. papers.title: Notation3: Graph Terms for RDF
papers.summary: Notation3 Logic was introduced as an extension of RDF allowing the user to express rules on top of triples and to make statements about graphs. The original proposal of the logic only came with an informal specification of its semantics which has been refined later on. While this refinement clarified the meaning of rules and implicitly quantified variables, it left the meaning of graphs used as terms - so-called graph terms - open. In this paper we aim to close this gap. We discuss in detail, how graph terms are used in Notation3, which formal requirements they need to meet, and provide examples to illustrate the difficulties when defining their semantics. We then introduce an abstract syntax for the logic and define its semantics in two steps: similarly to RDF's simple interpretations, we define interpretations and basic entailment for Notation3 which covers plain RDF triples but also triples containing graph terms. N3-entailment is then an extension of basic entailment which assigns meaning to the different special predicates of the logic like for example the implication symbol. N3-entailment is defined in a way that it can be extended whenever a new predicate is added to the logic. As Notation3 Logic is currently under development, we expect many predicates to be added. Our research provides and important step towards the full standardisation of the logic.

papers.title: Can Entanglement-Induced Feature-Map Designs Improve Projected Quantum Kernels?
papers.summary: Projected quantum kernels (PQKs) have emerged as a notable approach to circumvent the hardness of machine learning tasks arising from the exponential dimensionality of the quantum Hilbert space. The results show that extensive tuning can lead to competitive performance architectures, while our proposed entanglement topologies exhibit a significantly stronger native inductive bias. papers.title: Calibrated uncertainty quantification for prosumer flexibility aggregation in ancillary service markets
papers.summary: Reliable forecasting of prosumer flexibility is critical for demand response aggregators in frequency controlled ancillary service markets, where reliability requirements such as the P90 standard are enforced. Under nominal test conditions, conformal methods substantially improve joint coverage over uncalibrated MCD baselines. More conservative methods satisfy the 90% lower-tail reliability requirement, while CQR and multivariate CP (MCP) yield narrower intervals and higher economic value, retaining approximately 69% and 68% of perfect-information profit, respectively, under the stricter penalty interpretation. A controlled robustness analysis shows that increasing perturbations of load, solar, price, and activation inputs increase overbidding and reduce coverage and economic performance. The results highlight the trade-off between reliability, economic value, and robustness to input uncertainty in aggregator bidding.

papers.title: Confidence and Calibration of Activation Oracles for Reliable Interpretation of Language Model Internals
papers.summary: An activation oracle is a language model trained to convert the activations of another model into natural language. However, it is so far unclear to what extent these verbalizations are calibrated. Crucially, the oracle's verbalization come without any measure of confidence. Here, we compare five methods for estimating the confidence of an activation oracle. Our experiments cover four oracles from two model families (Qwen and Gemma, from 8B to 27B parameters), tested on the secret word task, whereby the oracle is supposed to recover a secret word, that has been fine-tuned into a model but does not appear in the model outputs. Our results with $6{,}000$ samples per method/oracle combination show that the best calibration depends on the availability of a hypothesis space or a calibration set: When an assumed auditor can list the possible answers in advance, the oracle should score each candidate answer directly. Scoring the candidates gives a higher accuracy on every oracle and a confidence that separates correct from incorrect answers better than any other method. When the oracle has to write its answer as free text, the agreement over twenty sampled answers gives the best calibrated confidence, which needs only five labeled secret words to be tuned. When a calibration set is available, a rescaled probability of the answer is as good as re-sampling, at the cost of one generation instead of twenty. Asking the oracle to write a number for its confidence, on the other side, gives no useful signal on any oracle. Code and the patched trainer are available at https://github.com/federicotorrielli/probabilistic_activation_oracles.

papers.title: Manifold Sampling via Entropy Maximization
papers.summary: Sampling from constrained distributions has a wide range of applications, including in Bayesian optimization and robotics. Prior work establishes convergence and feasibility guarantees for constrained sampling, but assumes that the feasible set is connected. However, in practice, the feasible set often decomposes into multiple disconnected components, which makes efficient sampling under constraints challenging. In this paper, we propose MAnifold Sampling via Entropy Maximization (MASEM) for uniform sampling on a manifold with an unknown number of disconnected components, implicitly defined by smooth equality and inequality constraints. The presented method uses a resampling scheme to maximize the entropy of the empirical distribution based on k-nearest neighbor density estimation. We show that, in the mean field, MASEM decreases the KL-divergence between the empirical distribution and the maximum-entropy target exponentially in the number of resampling steps. We instantiate MASEM with multiple local samplers and demonstrate its versatility and efficiency on synthetic and robotics-based benchmarks. MASEM enables fast and scalable mixing across a range of constrained sampling problems, improving over alternatives by an order of magnitude in Sinkhorn distance with competitive runtime.

papers.title: CrystalAR: Autoregressive Modeling for Symmetric Crystal Generation
papers.summary: Deep generative modeling has achieved remarkable progress in crystal generation. Given the rich symmetries inherent in crystalline structures, recent work has sought to explicitly incorporate space-group symmetry into generative models, enabling more effective exploration of novel symmetry templates. Yet introducing symmetry templates increases the combinatorial complexity of stoichiometric relationships between atomic species and crystallographic sites, while creating a fundamental tension between flexible exploration of discrete crystallographic templates and faithful realization of these templates as continuous three-dimensional structures. To address these challenges, we propose CrystalAR, a unified autoregressive framework that models Wyckoff symmetry templates and complete crystal structures within a single generative sequence. Specifically, CrystalAR reformulates continuous coordinate generation as a symmetry-conditioned hierarchy of discrete spatial localization decisions, autoregressively refining the positions of all symmetry-inequivalent sites across resolution levels while jointly modeling their spatial configuration within each level. This discrete hierarchical formulation further enables constraint-aware search over both crystallographic templates and geometric realizations. As a result, CrystalAR retains strong symmetry-template generation capability while achieving competitive de novo generation performance and template-free crystal structure prediction (CSP) accuracy. These results suggest that symmetry-template generation can be retained alongside broadly competitive de novo generation performance and competitive CSP without reliance on symmetry templates retrieved from prior data, providing a promising alternative paradigm for symmetry-preserving crystal generation.

papers.title: Network topology shapes consensus and vulnerability in LLM populations
papers.summary: As large language models (LLMs) are deployed in interacting populations, their collective behaviour depends not only on the models but also on who interacts with whom. Studies of convention formation in LLM populations have mainly tested well-mixed interactions. We place policies extracted from four LLMs on fully connected, random regular, and heterogeneous networks, with $10^3$ to $10^5$ agents playing the naming game. Topology affects how quickly consensus emerges, sometimes whether it emerges at all, and, in rare cases, which convention wins. Sparsest networks slow consensus up to twelvefold. Yet, by preserving correlations between persistent neighbours, they restore consensus in some cases that fail to converge under well-mixed interactions. Networks also govern vulnerability to adversarial attack. We measure the critical mass of committed agents needed to overturn an established convention. Tipping thresholds follow the same ordering across models and conditions: hubs $\leq$ random $\leq$ low-degree nodes. On the most heterogeneous topology, median critical masses are 3%, 16%, and 35%, respectively; targeting hubs requires one-sixth as many committed agents as random placement. For most models, networked populations are easier to tip than well-mixed ones, so well-mixed estimates can overstate robustness. Assessing the safety of multi-agent AI requires mapping who interacts with whom.

papers.title: PriMa-Causa: Causal Prescriptive Maintenance
papers.summary: Automated manufacturing requires data-driven decisions under uncertainty and sparse observational records, and unplanned downtime is a dominant cost of getting them wrong. Prescriptive maintenance recommends a maintenance action against an impending failure rather than merely predicting it. Established reference architectures couple predictive models with rule- or optimisation-based recommendation logic. Selecting a corrective action, however, requires an interventional quantity: how the line behaviour would change if the action were set. Manufacturing data is observational, so a model fitted to predict the outcome estimates an associational quantity and may misdirect the choice of action without the prediction error revealing it. Causal estimators target the interventional quantity but require an expert-led causal study per case, for which the bounded decision window of operation leaves no room. This dissertation analyses how causal reasoning can be embedded into prescriptive maintenance so that actions are ranked by their estimated interventional effect. The result is PriMa-Causa, built from three components: a causal reasoning layer that integrates the estimate into the PriMa reference model, a parametric simulator that supplies the interventional ground truth absent from manufacturing data, and a graph-conditioned tabular causal foundation model that, pre-trained once on this synthetic production-line prior, answers interventional queries in a single forward pass. PriMa-Causa attains a lower prescription error than associational baselines, with the largest margin under weak overlap and sparse context, and a partially disclosed causal graph reduces this error further. The causal inductive bias of the synthetic prior and the graph conditioning can thus replace per-case estimator fitting, a step toward automating causal inference for autonomous and self-healing maintenance.

papers.title: SetCommit: Coordinated Token Commitments for Few-Step Diffusion Language Model Decoding

Instead of selecting tokens independently by confidence, SetCommit selects a commitment set that balances token reliability against local joint commitment risk, preserving conditioning opportunities for subsequent denoising steps. papers.title: SDS-LoRA: Overcoming Anisotropic Gradient Scaling in Low-Rank Adaptation
papers.summary: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) enables efficient adaptation of large pretrained models to downstream tasks by parameterizing weight updates with low-rank matrices. We argue that this phenomenon is undesirable because it distorts the full fine-tuning gradient by skewing it toward dominant singular directions while suppressing others. Our analyses demonstrate that anisotropic gradient scaling reduces the effective rank of the low-rank matrices' gradients and fails to provide the best possible alignment between the full fine-tuning gradient and its low-rank approximation in LoRA for arbitrary gradients, thereby exacerbating the gap to full fine-tuning. To address these limitations, we propose a new low-rank parameterization, SDS-LoRA, which Structurally Decouples Singular values from the backward pass. Our method ensures that the full fine-tuning gradient backpropagates only through the orthonormal bases of the low-rank matrices' subspaces, independent of their scales. Convergence analysis demonstrates that while LoRA's convergence rate degrades with the condition number of the low-rank matrices, that of SDS-LoRA remains independent of it. Experimental results across natural language and vision benchmarks show that SDS-LoRA improves loss convergence and reduces the gap to full fine-tuning, significantly enhancing adaptation performance.

papers.title: Who Is the Influencer? Consensus Dynamics in Multi-Agent Systems
papers.summary: Multi-agent LLM systems are increasingly used in practice, but their behavior is complex and hard to understand. papers.title: Co-Recursive Semantic Self-Extension: A Mathematical Foundation for Open-Ended Intelligence
papers.summary: Artificial intelligence has advanced through scale, data, and computation, yet remains bounded by its representational framework. We ask what makes intelligence open-ended. Every inferential system selects meaningful distinctions, limiting what it can learn. Within a fixed purpose, performance reaches a ceiling set by its semantic domain. Teleological succession, in which purposes arise from earlier ones, faces a similar limit: Boolean-closed purpose-transformations exhaust their reachable semantic territory. We shift from purposes to inferential systems. Drawing on Kant and Gödel, we model cognitive states as partial evaluations over a formal language. Unresolved propositions may be undecided or undecidable. Reasoning can resolve the former but not the latter, leaving a frontier for extension. Non-trivial reductions of undecidable propositions expose undecidable intermediate premises whose reflective reification supports multiple decisive extensions. Finite trace-guided generation remains fallible, requiring meta-level selection and polycontextural exploration. Using Kolmogorov complexity, we show that no architecture with a fixed state description, transition mechanism, and initial condition can generate histories incorporating irreducible algorithmic information. Because physical systems are fixed in this sense, we examine collectives. Coupling finitely many finite agents does not remove the bound. Extension requires persistent external memory preserving semantic content and historical coordinates. Collective generative capacity depends on balancing overlap for transfer with difference for generation. We propose semantic self-extension as a design principle: intelligence should not merely resolve ambiguity within existing meanings, but transform unresolved structures into new spaces of meaning, generating new distinctions, questions, representations, and purposes.

papers.title: Multichoice Modeling: Exploring Decision Configuration Space under Uncertainty
papers.summary: Decision support has become sophisticated at exploring uncertainty, but much less so at representing the architecture of the decision itself. As a result, the decision space is often narrowed before uncertainty is analyzed, leaving interactions among choices and the effects of alternatives they imply largely invisible. Drawing on the logic of rugged landscapes, we conceptualize such problems as contingent performance landscapes, where interdependent choices generate configuration-specific outcomes whose value changes across uncertain futures. We demonstrate the framework through three case studies: a manufacturing process upgrade, M&A strategy, and mortgage design. By contrasting conventional uncertainty-only analysis with multichoice modeling, the cases show how opening the decision configuration space can reveal unexpected complementarities, near-best configurations with different risk profiles, and strategies that were not apparent as alternatives at the outset.

papers.title: Truthful by Omission: Click Thinning for LLM-Native Advertising
papers.summary: Generative AI assistants are becoming an advertising medium, embedding sponsored content in their answers. This setting departs from classical position auctions in two ways: an ad's click-through rate depends on the passage that hosts it, and because users stop at their first click, earlier ads take clicks from later ones. This competition for clicks makes truthfulness delicate: a higher bid can reshape the allocation and put a competitor ahead of the bidder, reducing the bidder's clicks. Existing mechanisms either attain a constant fraction of the optimal welfare (advertisers' total click value) but are not known to be truthful, or are truthful but their welfare guarantee degrades as the number of passages grows. We achieve both even when the answer and its editorial order are fixed before bidding. Assuming each ad's click-through rate when reached is known and unaffected by omitting other ads, we give a computationally efficient mechanism that is truthful in expectation and attains at least half the optimal welfare under free reordering. Our key idea, click thinning, omits ads at random, showing earlier ads less often so that each ad's overall click probability no longer depends on the order of the ads. Welfare maximization then reduces to a tractable matching problem, and solving it exactly with VCG-style payments makes truthful bidding optimal in expectation. Characterizing the click probabilities that omission can achieve sharpens the approximation factor from $2$ to $2-(1-δ)^{K-1}$ when at most $K$ ads are shown and each click-through rate is at most $δ$. This factor is the best possible for any order-preserving rule, even one that ignores incentives and computation, so truthfulness and computational efficiency incur no additional worst-case loss.

papers.title: Where Polanyi Meets Galois: Tacit Knowing as an Algebro-Deterministic Operation, Toward Re-rooting AI-Generated Science

This audit-valuation complementarity formalizes Polanyi's claim that tacit and explicit are not sharply divided. It separates contingent tacitness, which a new query brings out (AlphaGo's game tree), from regime-bound tacitness, statable only once it is gone (AlphaGo's hunches). (1) Polanyi's from-to structure reads as non-commutative binding. (2) Explicating the valuation destroys it, as with Polanyi's pianist, yet a closed-form law states it. Polanyi, Nonaka, Tsoukas and Collins each capture part of this, narrowly; even Nonaka and von Krogh's continuum cannot tell the classes apart. (3) Collins's three tacit knowledges become strata, one outside the substrate. (4) Our mentor-student DAG is a tacit-transmission graph. (5) Tao's remark that AI-solved problems spawn few follow-ups reveals rootless explicit knowledge: checkable results no one can trace or yet understands. To re-root them, LLMs generate, VaCoAl/PyVaCoAl keeps an auditable trace with its confidence, and people value, a role virtue epistemology shows cannot be offloaded. Art, craft and skill show the same decoupling of form from the maker's becoming. papers.title: OpenAttention: One Percent Is Enough with Tail Proxies
papers.summary: Sparse attention reads only a small subset of the key-value cache, and how to treat the unread tail remains a key challenge. Additionally, unlike prior methods that rank clusters by centroid alone, ErrorGate allocates the exact read by the estimated weight error of each cluster. papers.title: ACTIVA: Amortized Causal Effect Estimation via Variational Autoencoders

papers.title: DConstrain: Compiling Context-Parameterized Transitions for Diffusion Language Model Constrained Decoding
papers.summary: Diffusion language models (DLMs) decode multiple tokens in parallel, so individually valid tokens can be incompatible together under a schema. At runtime, warm compilation binds reached configurations to these programs to construct exact successors, overlapping with the model forward pass because graph construction requires no model scores. Furthermore, token-effect grouping merges tokens with identical compiled effects before runtime contexts are bound, so groups are reused across stacks and environments even when concrete successors differ. papers.title: Parameter Learning in Active Inference via Variational Message Passing
papers.summary: Active inference casts perception, learning and planning as variational inference, where the Expected Free Energy (EFE) defines the planning objective. Recent work showed that EFE minimization can be written as Variational Free Energy (VFE) minimization on a generative model augmented with epistemic priors, and that the resulting entropy-corrected objective is minimized by sum-product message passing (SP-MP) on modified factor functions. These formulations treat model uncertainty as inference over a finite set of known models. We extend them to planning during learning, where beliefs over the observation and transition parameters $θ_A$, $θ_B$ are Dirichlet priors. Closed-form Dirichlet updates are usually obtained by a structured mean-field factorization between parameters and states, but under exactly that factorization the information-gain corrections vanish. We resolve this by giving every factor its own parameter prior, frozen during a rollout. Conjugacy then makes each factor belief a product of a marginal over the categorical variables and a one-step Bayes posterior of the parameters. papers.title: Parallelizable Probabilistic Latent Reasoning for Diverse Reasoning Trajectories
papers.summary: Language models relying on verbalized Chain-of-Thought (CoT) are constrained to token-by-token generation in the language space, where many tokens serve textual coherence rather than core reasoning. This entangles genuine differences in logical trajectories with superficial variations in verbalization. However, current latent models remain largely deterministic, capturing only a single reasoning trajectory rather than modeling a distribution over multiple valid alternatives. While stochastic approaches parameterize distributions over latent reasoning steps, they frequently suffer from unstable optimization and limited empirical performance. Furthermore, their reliance on autoregressive latent prediction during training precludes effective parallelization, leading to prohibitively long training times. To overcome these bottlenecks, we propose Probabilistic Latent Reasoning Models (PLRM), a parallelizable variational framework for probabilistic latent reasoning. PLRM adopts a JEPA-style objective in which the posterior infers latent distributions in parallel from observed reasoning trajectories, while the prior learns to predict the subsequent latent distribution via teacher forcing. To model heterogeneous reasoning processes, we introduce a discrete strategy variable together with a mixture-based prior, allowing the model to preserve the Gaussian-mixture structure induced by multiple distinct reasoning trajectories rather than collapsing them into a single Gaussian. Across diverse benchmarks, PLRM achieves performance competitive with deterministic latent reasoning models on single-trajectory datasets while enabling efficient training and consistently outperforming competing stochastic baselines on multi-trajectory datasets.

papers.title: Survival is the Only Reward: Sustainable Self-Training Through Environment-Mediated Selection
papers.summary: Self-training systems often degenerate due to the lack of an external criterion for judging data quality, leading to reward hacking and semantic drift. This paper provides a proof-of-concept system architecture for stable self-training under sparse external feedback and bounded memory, and empirically characterises its learning dynamics and failure modes. We introduce a self-training architecture in which learning is mediated exclusively by environmental viability, rather than by reward, objective functions, or externally defined fitness criteria. Candidate behaviours are executed under real resource constraints, and only those whose environmental effects both persist and preserve the possibility of future interaction are propagated. The environment does not provide semantic feedback, dense rewards, or task-specific supervision; selection operates solely through differential survival of behaviours as world-altering events, making proxy optimisation impossible and rendering reward-hacking evolutionarily unstable. Analysis of semantic dynamics shows that improvement arises primarily through the persistence of effective and repeatable strategies under a regime of consolidation and pruning, a paradigm we refer to as negative-space learning (NSL), and that models develop meta-learning strategies (such as deliberate experimental failure in order to elicit informative error messages) without explicit instruction. This work establishes that environment-grounded selection enables sustainable open-ended self-improvement, offering a viable path toward more robust and generalisable autonomous systems without reliance on human-curated data or complex reward shaping.

papers.title: Bifurcations from Weight Space: JEPAWG on Parametric Dynamical Systems
papers.summary: Trained network weights are increasingly treated as data, but there is rarely ground truth about what a population of models should encode, which hampers systematic validation of weight-space methods. It was first introduced for neural samplers for lattice field theories, where its latent geometry located the phase transition and estimated the 2D Ising critical exponent. Applied to dynamical systems, JEPAWG is competitive on forecasting with a hypernetwork trained directly for that task, despite being supervised on the parameter--weight correspondence rather than on forecasts. Beyond forecasting, the norm of the parameter-derivative of the decoded weights locates Hopf points and curves, tracks a period-doubling cascade closely enough to give a qualitative estimate of the Feigenbaum constant, and detects a global bifurcation, which has no eigenvalue signature and is therefore invisible to linearisation. As such, JEPAWG provides interpretable insight into the dynamics that is not available from other hypernetworks. Together, these results indicate that JEPAWG is a workable instrument for reading physical structure off a population of trained networks.

papers.title: VLTest: Finding Joint Image-Text Failures in Vision-Language Models
papers.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly embedded in software systems. Testing them raises two problems. papers.title: ProQuant: Preserving Expert Quality over Quantity in Ultra-Low-Bit Quantization of Mixture-of-Experts Models
papers.summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) large language models reduce computation through sparse activation but still incur substantial storage costs. papers.title: Abstract Priorities, Concrete Rewards: How Stated Preferences Relate to What People Reward in AI Responses

papers.title: Trajectory Learnability for Offline On-Policy Distillation with Imperfect Teachers
papers.summary: Offline on-policy distillation gains efficiency by collecting student trajectories and teacher supervision once and reusing them throughout optimization. The same reuse makes imperfect supervision persistent. A natural alternative is to estimate teacher recoverability along the trajectory, but repeated continuations largely erase the efficiency advantage of offline distillation. We instead use teacher-successful problems to define a cheap reference for what the student can learn. We train on teacher-successful problems and measure how the likelihood of each observed token in trajectories from teacher-failed problems changes. We use these signed likelihood changes as an operational \emph{learnability signal}: larger increases indicate behavior more strongly promoted by successful-only learning. We aggregate this signal into trajectory-level weights for the original distillation loss. Unlike continuation-based estimates, our learnability requires no additional generation and can be computed once from stored trajectories and model checkpoints. papers.title: ULME: Predictive Coupling for Mutually Reinforcing Embedding and Language Modeling
papers.summary: Text embedding and text generation are two of the most useful capabilities of modern large language models, yet they are typically provided by separate specialized models (an embedder and a generator) trained with incompatible objectives and deployed side by side in retrieval-augmented generation and agent systems. papers.title: Scaling Laws for Safety Probes
papers.summary: Safety probes trained on a model's activations are a standard tool for monitoring language models in real time. Each time a new model is released or a new harm area needs to be monitored, the probe must be retrained, which requires new labels and a choice of probe architecture. Yet neither the model nor the labels tell us in advance how well the resulting probe will perform. Finding out requires training and comparing many probe configurations. In this paper, we ask whether probe performance can instead be predicted in advance from model size and the number of labels. Existing safety datasets are insufficient for this, as they are either limited in scale or already saturated. We therefore construct six new safety datasets of sufficient size and difficulty. On these datasets, we train two probe architectures on 20 base models from five model families, with 32 to $10^{6}$ labels for each model. We measure performance using probe error, defined as 1 - AUROC, where lower values are better. We find that probe error follows two simple scaling laws. First, the lowest probe error a model can reach falls as a power law in its size. Second, probe error decreases towards its floor as the number of examples increases; the slope increases as the target model size increases. Both laws hold across tasks, model families and probe architectures, and only their fitted constants differ. When fitted on the smallest models of a family, the laws predict the error of the next larger model to within 0.02 in 72% of cases. They also identify whether more labels or a larger model is the cheaper way to reach a target error in 73% of cases. Finally, they choose the probe architecture with an extra error of only 0.006 on average when they pick the worse one. These laws allow safety researchers to determine how to create the best probe for any given model and label budget.

papers.title: MarkTune: Improving the Quality-Detectability Trade-off in Model-Embedded LLM Watermarking
papers.summary: Language model watermarking schemes fall into two broad categories: inference-time methods, which modify the decoding process at generation time, and model-embedded methods, which encode a secret signal directly into the model weights. Empirically, MarkTune substantially improves the quality-detectability frontier of GaussMark, approaching the detectability of strong inference-time schemes while preserving generation quality and downstream task performance. papers.title: Stop Drawing Scientific Claims from LLM Social Simulations Without Robustness Audits
papers.summary: The scientific claims drawn from LLM social simulations should be no stronger than the robustness audits that support them. Generative agents bring new expressive power to agent-based modeling, enabling simulations of collective social processes like cooperation, polarization, and norm formation. Yet they also introduce complexity through additional architectural choices, such as agent specification, memory representation, interaction protocols, and environment design. Small perturbations that appear minor to researchers can cascade into macro-level outcomes through repeated interaction, creating a "butterfly effect." Consequently, scientific claims drawn from LLM social simulations may reflect implementation artifacts rather than the social mechanisms being modeled. We support this position with two case studies: a repeated Prisoner's Dilemma and a social media echo chamber simulation. Across multiple models, minor perturbations in persona format and game-instruction framing shift cooperation rates by up to 76 percentage points, while network homophily and hub assignment produce significant and consistent shifts in polarization metrics. We also find that sensitivity is unevenly distributed across both architectural choices and model families: the same perturbation that produces the 76 pp shift in one frontier model only shifts another by 1 pp. Robustness is therefore a property that should be measured per claim and per model, not assumed. To address this validation gap, we introduce TRAILS (Taxonomy for Robustness Audits In LLM Simulations), a robustness-audit taxonomy spanning three levels of simulation design: agent (micro-level), interaction (meso-level), and system (macro-level). We call for robustness to become a first-order validation requirement before LLM social simulations are used to explain mechanisms, evaluate interventions, or inform decisions.

papers.summary: Prediction error is widely used to evaluate nuisance-function estimators in causal inference, but its relationship with the performance of the resulting causal estimator is not well understood. We evaluated nuisance-function prediction error, bias, RMSE, and 95% confidence interval coverage, and derived the second-order remainder through which errors in the exposure and outcome nuisance functions jointly determine the bias of the residualized estimator. When all methods estimated the causal effect from the same training sample, DML-XGBoost had the lowest RMSE and the highest coverage among the non-oracle methods, although XGBoost fitted to the full training sample had lower out-of-sample prediction error for both nuisance functions. GAMs had the lowest prediction error of all methods but were biased, with coverage of 0.55 with independent observations. The remainder reproduced the average bias of OLS, GAMs, and DML-XGBoost, but only half to three-quarters of the bias of XGBoost, whose residuals were formed on the data used to fit it. A joint-error measure based on the absolute cross-product of the two nuisance errors was only weakly associated with causal bias. Prediction error is useful for assessing nuisance-function estimation, but it should not be treated as a direct measure of the quality of the resulting causal estimator.

papers.title: SplatLab: Autonomous Scientific Discovery for 3DGS Research
papers.summary: Reproducing a published 3DGS paper takes weeks of expert engineering before any extension can be proposed. Given a research prompt, a target-paper URL, or no input at all, it reproduces a published baseline, proposes an extension, trains and ablates across Mip-NeRF 360 and LLFF, writes the manuscript, and binds every reported number to a logged training run. papers.title: Same Beliefs, Different Policies: Learning Reusable Representations for Early Stopping in LLM Reasoning
papers.summary: Reasoning LLMs often continue reasoning after reaching a correct answer, wasting computation and sometimes replacing it with an incorrect one. In all three domains, its accuracy-cost trade-offs are competitive with or better than those of end-to-end controllers. papers.title: FlashBoB: I/O-Efficient Exact Backward-over-Backward for Softmax Attention
papers.summary: Transformer models built on the attention mechanism have become a central building block in modern deep learning, yet softmax attention remains a major bottleneck for long-context workloads. While FlashAttention makes the forward and first backward passes I/O-efficient, it does not support backward-over-backward (BoB), which enables exact differentiation through the backward pass for applications such as second-order optimization, test-time training, gradient-based memory, and meta-learning. Existing BoB implementations either materialize large intermediate tensors or exhaust GPU memory at long sequence lengths. We present FlashBoB, an exact, I/O-efficient algorithm for BoB in softmax attention that keeps computation within on-chip tiles and avoids all $N \times N$ intermediate tensors, where $N$ is the sequence length. The key insight is a hierarchical affine structure in the softmax double backward: two row-wise scalars determine all outputs through affine transformations. This yields a two-pass schedule with bounded on-chip static random-access memory (SRAM) usage and minimal off-chip high-bandwidth memory (HBM) traffic. FlashBoB achieves $Θ(N^2 d^2/M)$ HBM traffic ($d$ is the head dimension and $M$ is the memory size) and, within the standard FlashAttention-style score-recomputation model, matches the inherited large-cache lower bound for exact forward attention. Empirically, it scales exact attention BoB to $N=262\text{K}$ on a single A100 80GB GPU, where prior PyTorch exact baselines fail by $N=16\text{K}$, and is up to $6.3\times$ faster than FlashBack. These results make exact second-order attention practical at long-context sequence lengths where prior implementations cannot run efficiently.

papers.title: Agent Mosaic: Recognizing Confidentiality Leaks in Agentic LLM Systems
papers.summary: Modern LLM agents can retrieve information from accessible documents, and then disclose a sensitive conclusion assembled from them. This mosaic effect creates a critical risk for agents operating over confidential data. Even under benign queries designed to be answerable from one document, GPT-5.6-Sol, the best performing model tested, discloses forbidden composites in 7.08% of answers (95% CI: 3.75-10.67%) in simulation, with worse disclosure rates in live harnesses. Adding visible classification headers and explicit aggregation rules reduces pooled disclosure rates substantially, yet unsafe disclosures persist in 32.37% of simulated answers (95% CI: 28.33-36.19%) across all intents despite these safeguards. Furthermore, increased refusals do not guarantee confidentiality, since significant refusals reveal the prohibited conclusion regardless. These results point to a troubling conclusion: sensitive data leaks via mosaic-style events are an observed confidentiality failure mode in the evaluated settings at non-negligible rates. They motivate stronger controls on what agents may infer and disclose in sensitive data environments with mixed-clearance users.

papers.title: Behavioral Consistency in Machine Learning
papers.summary: A trained model is usually described by its weights, as if the weights fixed its behavior. In practice the same weights are run by different programs. Training uses high-precision accumulation and fixed tensor shapes, while serving uses low-precision arithmetic, fused attention kernels, a paged key-value cache, and dynamic batching. These programs produce different next-token distributions from identical weights. We make this dependence explicit by indexing a policy by the kernel that executes it, and we propose kernel contracts, which state how far a serving kernel may drift from a reference kernel on each slice of traffic and what the serving system should do when a limit is exceeded. We prove non-asymptotic bounds that link the logit difference between two kernels to total-variation and KL divergence, to the change in expected reward, to the bias of policy gradients computed from rollouts generated by another kernel, and to whether the greedy token can change. We test the bounds and the contracts in GPU experiments on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with Hugging Face and vLLM. The bounds hold on every prompt we measured. Lower precision, a different serving engine, and a different batch size each change the generated token on some prompts, and these changes concentrate on prompts where the model is nearly undecided between two tokens. A kernel can therefore look fine on aggregate metrics while behaving differently on exactly these prompts. Checking a contract separately on each slice of traffic catches these cases.

papers.title: Probing and Steering for Safety-Relevant Behaviours in Large Language Models
papers.summary: Activation probes are computed directions in a language model's residual stream, used both to detect safety-relevant behaviours and, by adding their direction back into the stream, to steer them. The pipeline crosses two estimators (difference-of-means and logistic regression) with three token-pooling schemes (last, mean and learned attention), selects appropriate layers to detect or steer a behaviour, and evaluates every direction twice: as a detector of the behaviour, and as a steering vector to push outputs towards the behaviour. Prior work read together suggests a read/write dissociation, in which logistic regression reads (detects) best but difference-of-means directions write (steer) best. We find that it holds for deception and high-stakes but not for sycophancy, where the pattern reverses. The reversal appears to follow partially from the data rather than from the estimators. The best pooling technique and the layer choice depend on the behaviour and data, and the layer that steers best can sit well before the layer that detects best. The right steering metric to use between changing a model's perception and eliciting behaviour depends on the task - and the two can disagree outright. The exported probes and directions power an interactive interface through which a user can score and steer text directly.

papers.title: Gender, Sexual Orientation, and the One-Year Refugee Bar: A Computational Study of Bill C-12 and Canadian Refugee Adjudication
papers.summary: In March 2026, Bill C-12 amended the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act to make refugee claims ineligible for referral to the Refugee Protection Division where they are made more than one year after the claimant's first entry to Canada. The results of this study demonstrate that, first, while most claimants claim within a year, roughly one in nine in the published record does not, and gender and SOGIE claims are significantly overrepresented among these late claims. Second, among late claims, refusals of gender and SOGIE claims are more likely than refusals of other claims to be overturned on appeal or judicial review. Late claims on other grounds, by contrast, fare somewhat worse on review than timely claims. The one-year bar therefore removes the hearing, the appeal, and the stay from the late claimants for whom those safeguards have been doing the most work. papers.title: Breaking the high-degree barrier in Lehmer's problem with a human-AI discovery loop
papers.summary: While artificial intelligence has made rapid progress in mathematical reasoning, many open problems depend on structure that is revealed only through large-scale computational exploration and analytical synthesis. One such example is Lehmer's problem from 1933. It asks whether the Mahler measure of an integer polynomial, which measures how far its roots stray from the unit circle, can be made arbitrarily small. Previously, constructing irreducible polynomials with integer coefficients and small Mahler measure has been carried out systematically only for even degrees $d \le 180$. At higher degrees, Boyd's analytical one-parameter family frequently factors, skipping nearly 50% of target degrees and leaving no general construction for arbitrary $d$. Here, we address the high-degree regime through a human-AI discovery loop, in which we extend the conversational prompting with a fast numerical pipeline, an exact symbolic verifier, and large-scale distributed search. The AI agent prototypes numerical and symbolic solvers locally, launches parallel searches across distributed clusters and works with the human researcher to extract and verify mathematical hypotheses. Through this interactive loop, we derive a five-parameter construction, which we call the Generalized Boyd algorithm. It eliminates degree-skipping and constructs irreducible polynomials with Mahler measure strictly below Boyd's limit point $α_1 \approx 1.255434$ for every target degree. Evaluated across all even degrees up to 2000, our approach improves upon six previously published values and holds 99.6% of all best known records. With this work we release the verified dataset of polynomials with minimal Mahler measure across all studied even degrees.

papers.title: Think Harder Where It Matters: Item-Level Adaptive Recursion for Sequential Recommendation
papers.summary: Existing sequential recommenders usually allocate a fixed computational budget to every item in a user's interaction history, regardless of the item's contribution to the final prediction. We challenge this de facto design with two diagnostic findings. (1) Non-uniform computational need: items within the same sequence vary drastically in how much computation they require. Most converge after shallow processing while a critical minority only stabilizes at full depth. (2) Suboptimality of fixed allocation: given oracle access to the target item, a non-uniform depth assignment consistently outranks the fixed one, indicating that existing uniform computation both wastes capacity on already-converged items and sacrifices overall recommendation quality. These observations motivate a shift from fixed-depth computation to item-level adaptive reasoning. To this end, we propose LoopRec. LoopRec recursively applies a single weight-shared block and introduces a lightweight gate at each recursion boundary that makes a binary exit-or-continue decision for every item independently. Items whose representations have sufficiently matured exit early, while those requiring deeper reasoning continue to subsequent recursions. papers.title: Parallel AI Agent Collaboration as Graph-Structured Distributed Block Optimization
papers.summary: Parallel AI agents can produce useful local edits yet degrade a shared solution when their edits are combined. papers.title: HiddenLens: A Multi-Layer LLM Framework for Detecting and Resolving Hidden Assumptions in Software Requirements
papers.summary: Natural-language software requirements often omit assumptions about performance, operating conditions, user behaviour, and domain constraints, affecting architecture, testing, and deployment. papers.summary: While de-identification models can help conceal the identity of the individuals mentioned in a document, they fail to address linkage risks, defined as the potential to map the de-identified text back to its source. One straightforward way to perform such linkages is to extract phrases from the de-identified document and check their presence in the original dataset. We first construct an inverted index of the N-grams occurring in the text collection, making it possible to efficiently determine which N-grams appear in fewer than $k$ documents, either alone or in combination with other N-grams. An LLM-based rewriter is then iteratively queried to reformulate those spans until linkage is no longer possible. Experimental results on two datasets (court cases and Wikipedia biographies) show that the rewriting method can effectively prevent search-based linkages while remaining faithful to the original content. However, we also highlight that linkages remain feasible with the help of more advanced, semantics-oriented approaches.

papers.title: PAUSE: Search-Free Steering of Coding Agents Before Their First Source-Code Edit
papers.summary: Coding agents can invest substantial effort in repository exploration and testing yet still produce unsuccessful patches. papers.title: Broadband Mid-Wave Infrared Imaging Enabled by All-Silicon Hyperboloid Metalens
papers.summary: The mid-wave infrared (MWIR, 3-5 microns) is indispensable for thermal sensing, gas detection, long-range imaging, and free-space optical communications. papers.title: Language Models Give Group-Linked Fields the Wrong Weight
papers.summary: Large language models are increasingly used to judge people, and their answers can depend on inputs correlated with a protected attribute such as race, even when that attribute is never shown. Interpreting this reliance requires knowing how much predictive information those inputs add, but audits often report only whether a decision changes. We introduce an evidence-referenced audit that compares proxy reliance with two references, the known outcome rule and a Bayesian linear regression fitted to the same labeled examples, while measuring ranking accuracy separately. We apply it to four models in a simulated patient-ranking task with known field weights. We find four results. First, at zero predictive value, the models still relied on fields that carried no information, while the same-example learner did not. Second, as proxies became predictive, reliance grew far less than the reference. Third, display format mattered. Ordered labels drew more reliance than arbitrary labels, a direction that held in all four models. Fourth, ranking accuracy did not consistently track these changes in reliance. Based on these findings, we argue that decision changes and accuracy cannot show whether proxy reliance is warranted by the evidence. Audits should report reliance against an explicit predictive reference, alongside accuracy. Ordered fields whose values move with group membership, such as scores or income bands, are a useful starting point. Together, these results make it possible to measure how far reliance departs from the evidence, rather than infer it from observed choices alone.

papers.title: S-EDL: Eliciting Self-Evidence from Sequence Likelihoods for Semantic Calibration of LLMs

papers.title: MemoryTax: The Bitter Lesson of Agent Memory

papers.title: Prediction Is Not Calibration: Item Parameter Recovery and Representation Coupling in Knowledge Tracing
papers.summary: Knowledge tracing (KT) models can estimate item parameters through an item response decoder trained solely for next-response prediction, yet predictive accuracy does not guarantee parameter recovery. papers.title: COMET: A coordinated multi-layer runtime monitoring framework for human-supervised AI-enabled safety systems
papers.summary: Incorporating AI systems into safety systems requires monitoring to avoid silent faults and ensure safe and reliable operation. Single monitors often do not provide actionable information for human supervisors, who act as the system's adaptive controller. We present COMET, a coordinated multi-layer runtime monitoring framework for human-supervised AI-enabled safety systems in which each monitor is anchored in a different fault mode. Monitor outputs are combined in a coordination layer and mapped by a communication layer to a traffic-light display. In this work, COMET consists of three monitoring layers: signal integrity, physics consistency, and the AI system's competence envelope. The framework is evaluated on an open dataset of compressed-air leaks, where an AI system detects leaks from acoustic emissions, with held-out conditions simulating covariate shift, semantic shift, and sensor faults, events expected during runtime but unknown in their exact appearance. All monitors are frozen after development and tested zero-shot, and the framework is compared against no-monitoring and single-monitor setups. The bare AI system fails silently and confidently under all three shift types, whereas COMET reduces the trusted-wrong-answer rate to zero on covariate-shifted no-leak data and on three of four sensor faults, at a nominal false-alarm rate of $\approx 1\%$. Single monitors come close in detection but cannot attribute the fault mode. COMET converts their anonymous detection flags into diagnoses. Residual silent misses under semantic shift define the boundary of passive monitoring. papers.title: InfoQuant: Shaping Activation Distributions for Low-Bit LLM Quantization
papers.summary: Low-bit activation quantization remains a major bottleneck in efficient large language model (LLM) deployment. The difficulty is not only that activations contain outliers, but that their distributions are often poorly matched to a low-bit uniform quantizer. Existing post-training quantization (PTQ) methods suppress peaks, balance channels, or minimize reconstruction error, yet they rarely specify what activation distribution is actually easy to discretize. As a result, activations may appear numerically smoother while still incurring large quantization error because the quantization range remains wide or most values collapse into a few levels near the mean. We recast activation transformation as quantizer-facing distribution design and analyze quantization error from an information-theoretic perspective. Our analysis shows that quantization-friendly activations should jointly have a smaller numerical range and sufficient dispersion within that range. Guided by this analysis, we propose InfoQuant, a train-free method that employs Peak Suppression Orthogonal Transformation (PSOT) to shape activations into more quantization-friendly distributions. We further introduce adaptive outlier-token selection to improve the robustness of PSOT during optimization. Across multiple LLM families, InfoQuant consistently outperforms prior PTQ and end-to-end training baselines. Under W4A4KV4, it preserves 97% of floating-point accuracy on average and reduces the LLaMA-2 13B performance gap by 42% over the previous state of the art. papers.title: Learning What to Remember: Resource-Efficient Self-Improvement for Lifelong Agents
papers.summary: Self-improving agents aim to continuously improve their behavior by learning from experience after deployment. However, accumulating and reusing more experience does not necessarily lead to better decisions, particularly when generation, interaction, and memory resources are jointly constrained. Without updating the backbone model, TokenWorth uses the learned worth to guide both experience retrieval and bounded memory management, enabling the agent to continually adapt how it reuses accumulated experience. Across three LifelongAgentBench environments and both local and API-based deployments, TokenWorth achieves the highest task success rate while using the fewest output tokens among the evaluated methods under the specified resource budgets. These results suggest that effective self-improvement under resource constraints depends not on accumulating more experience, but on learning what is worth remembering. papers.title: Where Do LLMs Learn to Recommend AI?
papers.summary: Asked what to study, which career to pursue, or what product to build, large language models (LLMs) often recommend AI-related options. papers.title: Graph-Theoretic Formulation of Hamiltonian and Ground-State Sign Structures in Heisenberg Antiferromagnets
papers.summary: We study Heisenberg antiferromagnets through a graph-theoretic representation of their Hamiltonians. In the computational basis of a fixed-magnetization sector, the Heisenberg Hamiltonian equals a constant minus the weighted Laplacian of a graph whose vertices are spin configurations and whose edges connect configurations related by exchanging two antiparallel spins on a lattice bond. We call this graph the Hilbert graph (HG) which is isomorphic to the token graph of the lattice over which the Hamiltonian is defined. The exact ground-state energy is then determined by the largest eigenvalue of the HG Laplacian, which is the spectral relaxation of weighted Max-Cut on the HG. With the amplitudes fixed, the phase-dependent part of the variational energy defines an antiferromagnetic classical XY model on the HG, with couplings set by the amplitudes. Restricting the variational state to be real, i.e., restricting its phases to $\{0,π\}$, reduces the fixed-amplitude energy minimization to solving an antiferromagnetic Ising model and hence a weighted Max-Cut on the HG. When the weights are generated from non-degenerate ground-state amplitudes, the optimal phases give the ground-state sign structure which can be recovered from the weights in time polynomial in the size of the HG. On the Hamiltonian side, a diagonal sign transformation removes all positive off-diagonal matrix elements if and only if the HG is bipartite, which reproduces the Marshall sign rule on bipartite lattices through the graph two-coloring problem; otherwise, the minimal remaining positive weight equals the sum of HG edge weights left uncut by the Max-Cut. This graph formulation establishes a common framework for understanding wave function sign structure, Hamiltonian stoquasticity, non-convexity of phase optimization in variational Monte Carlo, and the average sign in quantum Monte Carlo.

papers.title: Lineage-Aware Search Control for LLM-Based Evolutionary Factor Mining
papers.summary: Formulaic alpha factor mining searches for symbolic expressions that transform market data into predictive signals. Recent LLM-based evolutionary factor mining methods use large language models as semantic variation operators. Under the conventional LLM-EA paradigm, stochastic variation and fitness-based selection can leave the search weakly directed and concentrated around a narrow set of structurally similar factors. We argue that these limitations arise because current methods mainly organize search at the individual and population levels, leaving lineage-level control underused. A lineage connects successive factor variants through evolutionary descent. We propose LineageEvo, which uses lineage in two coupled forms of search control: (1) lineage-conditioned LLM variation, which distills Lineage-Scoped Search Experience into operator-specific priors and fuses them with global operator priors, providing persistent, lineage-relevant guidance for LLM generation; and (2) lineage-stratified search allocation, which balances factor quality against lineage concentration by distributing the search budget across lineages during evolutionary search. Together, these mechanisms make semantic variation more direction aware and prevent branches from dominating the evolution, thereby promoting the discovery of predictive and diverse factors. We evaluate LineageEvo on CSI 500 and S&P 500 in terms of factor predictiveness, portfolio performance, search efficiency, and lineage- and expression-level diversity. LineageEvo achieves the strongest predictive performance on both markets, while LSPS produces a more balanced lineage distribution and a structurally broader factor pool. The results support lineage as a useful intermediate unit for controlling LLM-based evolutionary factor search.

papers.title: Feedback That Backfires in Games: Do LLM Players Repeat the Move They Just Watched Fail?
papers.summary: When an LLM agent's move fails, the harness writes the move and the failure message into the transcript and asks again. In tool calling, this record makes small models more likely to repeat the failed action. We test whether the same holds in games (Sokoban, Connect Four, Othello), where a move can fail by being illegal or by being legal but losing, both verified exactly. On fixed probe items built by perturbing a correct move, the record backfires: pooled over 8 instruction-tuned models (135M-1.7B) it makes the failed move more likely (corrective gain G = -1.38 nats per token), through the move's surface form, for illegal moves but not for losing ones, and not for every model. An exploratory analysis shows what sets the sign: after the record, the failed move's log-probability barely depends on how likely it was before (slope 0.18). Moves the model would not have played become more likely, and greedy decoding starts to produce them; moves it was about to play become less likely, but greedy decoding still repeats 38% of them. A description of the failure that omits the move string keeps the model's preference instead. Along the OLMo 2 1B post-training ladder the inversion is present in the base model and largely removed at the DPO stage. RAGEN's default models invert in RAGEN's own Sokoban format before any RL. A "do not repeat" instruction does nothing, a clean retry is the worst harness, and a decoder ban stops exact repeats but not illegal play. All measurements ran in float32 on a free Colab GPU, which first reproduced the original paper's number.

papers.title: Improved Training of Strong Stochastic Flow Maps

papers.title: The Reflexivity Threshold: A Phase Transition for Multi-Agent Performative Prediction
papers.summary: Many learning systems are performative: once deployed, their predictions change the data distribution on which future models are trained. In multi-agent settings, this feedback is routed through a network of interacting learners, so stability depends not only on the strength of performativity but also on who affects whom. Prior work often collapses cross-agent feedback into a scalar contraction constant, missing this network structure. We instead introduce the reflexivity matrix $Γ$, which records how strongly one agent's deployment can move another agent's best response, defined from per-agent gradient sensitivities and curvature parameters. The threshold occurs when the spectral radius of this matrix crosses one. Below the threshold, repeated retraining converges geometrically to a unique performatively stable equilibrium, with cumulative excess loss bounded uniformly in the time horizon. Above the threshold, we construct noisy supercritical instances in which every local-information learner incurs expected cumulative excess loss growing linearly for horizons up to order $1/(ρ(Γ)-1)$. Together, these results characterize the threshold behavior through upper and lower bounds and recover the single-agent scalar threshold from prior work as a special case.

papers.title: Allocating Indivisible Goods to Strategic Agents: Pure Nash Equilibria and Fairness
papers.summary: We consider the problem of fairly allocating a set of indivisible goods to a set of strategic agents with additive valuation functions. We assume no monetary transfers and, therefore, a mechanism in our setting is an algorithm that takes as input the reported -- rather than the true -- values of the agents. Further, we show that a weaker version of the latter result holds for any mechanism for two agents that always has pure Nash equilibria which all induce EFX allocations.

papers.title: Mitigating Query Shortcuts in Chain-of-Thought with Context-Aware Decoding

papers.title: SUDP: Secret-Use Delegation Protocol for Agentic Systems
papers.summary: Agentic systems now act with user secrets for APIs, messaging platforms, and cloud services. Today's agent runtimes typically implement authorization by exposure: enabling action means placing a reusable secret, or a reusable artifact derived from it, inside the runtime, so a transient prompt-injection or tool-side compromise becomes durable account compromise. Existing defenses cover adjacent pieces such as secret storage, scoped delegation, sender-constrained tokens, and runtime monitoring, but none states the combined requirement: an untrusted autonomous requester should be able to cause a user-authorized secret-backed operation without gaining reusable authority over it. We formalize this as the Agent Secret Use (ASU) problem and identify seven security properties any solution must satisfy, spanning authorization integrity and secret confidentiality. We propose the Secret-Use Delegation Protocol (SUDP), in which a requester proposes a canonical operation, the user authorizes it with a fresh authenticator-backed grant, and a custodian redeems the grant to perform the bounded use; reusable authority never crosses the requester boundary. papers.title: A Theoretical Analysis of Why Masked Diffusion Models Mitigate the Reversal Curse
papers.summary: Autoregressive language models (ARMs) suffer from the reversal curse: after learning ''$A$ is $B$,'' they often fail on the reverse query ''$B$ is $A$.'' In a one-layer MDM, we prove that forward masked training strengthens evidence that is reusable in reverse queries, induces correlated forward--reverse attention routes, and yields a positively aligned shared-storage gradient component that decreases the reverse loss to first order. papers.title: Solving Go under Positional Superko: Sound Proof Transfer and New Board Values
papers.summary: Positional superko (PSK) forbids recreating any earlier whole-board position. It is part of the Chinese rules as written and of the rules used in computer Go. Yet almost all solved Go boards were computed under a simpler basic-ko rule set. PSK makes solving hard: legality depends on the whole game history, and this breaks the three tools that make solving tractable, namely transposition tables (the graph-history interaction problem), static life-and-death recognition, and safe move pruning. We present Sanko, a parallel depth-first proof-number solver that restores all three soundly. Its core is a cheap proof-transfer theorem: a stored proof stays valid on a new path unless a board that the proof's winner must create has already occurred. Sanko proves 5x5 Go in 16 minutes with six threads, where the previous state of the art needed 5.25 hours with six processes, and in about a minute and a half on one 192-thread machine. It also establishes the first PSK values of twenty-three further boards, eleven of which were unsolved under any rules. Superko changes game-theoretic values: 4x7, a full-board win under basic ko, is worth only 12 points under PSK, and we pinpoint the move at which the previously published optimal line fails. Unlike earlier solutions of empty Go boards, we release the solver source together with the command line and outcome of every run behind our values and measurements, so that all reported values can be reproduced.

papers.title: LLMSeg: Training-Free Text-Prompted Image Segmentation with B-Splines
papers.summary: Promptable segmentation models such as SAM 3 achieve remarkable open-vocabulary performance but require dedicated architectures, large-scale annotation engines, and task-specific training. papers.title: Detection Is Not Enough: Reasoning Traces as Testable Program Hypotheses
papers.summary: When a language model is deployed, no reference solution exists, so the reasoning trace it writes is the only evidence for judging its answer. The reference-free substitutes each fail differently: self-assessment degrades the answer it was meant to protect, sampling agreement measures stability rather than correctness, and perturbation studies read the expected answer off a human-written template, grading a model rather than a trace. We ask how far a single trace can be verified with no reference solution, no judge model and no weight update, and find, for a frozen LLaMA-2-7B-chat on GSM8K, that detection is not what limits such a pipeline. Checking a trace against itself reaches an AUROC of 0.741 and stops there for a structural reason: two thirds of wrong traces state no false equation, having executed a mistaken plan correctly, and on wrong-plan failures the detector flags a wrong trace less often than a right one. A candidate-derived metamorphic probe exposes many of these failures: we abstract the trace into a program over the question's quantities, perturb one quantity, execute the program, and ask the model the rewritten question once, so every trace supplies its own test. Valid perturbations exist for 937 of 1,319 test questions (71.0%); among the 847 that also have a parseable first trace, supported traces are correct 60.6% of the time against a 31.6% base rate, although the probe also refutes 45.5% of correct traces. No tested policy yields a statistically significant improvement in accuracy. A flag earns its retry only when detector precision exceeds D/(R+D), where R and D are the rates at which a retry repairs a wrong trace and damages a correct one; our repair rate is so low that, at the same retry budget, even a perfect detector would recover an estimated 66 of 1,319 questions. Repair, not detection, is the open problem.

papers.title: 2-Step Agent: How a Bayesian Decision Maker Learns from AI-Decision Support
papers.summary: Prognostic predictions from ML models support human decision making in several fields, including high-stakes ones such as healthcare and the judiciary. papers.title: RayCo4D: Ray-Conditioned Continuous Motion Model for Monocular 4D Dynamic Reconstruction

papers.title: Resuming Vision-Language Inference across Onboard Interruptions

papers.title: Correlated Failures of AI Approval Monitors
papers.summary: Before an AI agent takes a consequential action, such as paying, messaging or changing code, several monitors check it. Their verdicts are combined by aggregating scores or by counting approvals, whatever inputs the monitors share. Monitors that share a base model or a poisoned input, however, may fail together. Every reliable fooling of a monitor into approving a fraud came through an evidence source and reached only that source's readers. Fooling it into blocking a correct payment depended on injection resistance, a monitor's refusal to follow instructions planted in its data. Small models and DeepSeek obeyed such notes. The three closed models ignored them in all but one case, and Opus also resisted persuasion tailored to it. On new data, a rule that counts sources instead of votes blocked 0.9% of correct payments, against 7.4% for the best counting rule, at equal safety. The pre-registered worst-case test failed. One attack left the approvers on a single source, so no rule over the twelve language-model monitors survives every measured attack. Adding a rule engine, which cannot be persuaded, restored the condition for a safe and live rule on the measured attacks. Diversify the inputs, harden the monitors, count sources, not votes.

papers.title: Conditional Flow Models Convert Epistemic Uncertainty into Apparent Aleatoric Variance
papers.summary: Conditional Flow Models (CFMs) are increasingly being used in place of deterministic predictors across machine learning, including for tasks that were classically formulated as regression. Given their success in such tasks, we ask the question: what useful information do the conditional distributions produced by CFMs carry beyond what a point predictor would provide? We identify a systematic phenomenon: in many natural regimes, CFM samples routinely have larger variance than the true conditional distribution, even in nearly deterministic regression problems. This effect is most pronounced where the model has not resolved the dependence on the conditioning variable, and thus the additional variance can be viewed as converting epistemic uncertainty in fitting the ground truth conditional distribution into apparent aleatoric variance in the generated samples. Through controlled synthetic and real-data experiments, and comparisons with explicit smoothing estimators, we show that the induced variance tracks model underfitting of complex or hard-to-fit targets, and decreases with additional training or data. We provide a theoretical account of the phenomenon in a simplified setting and demonstrate a consequent practical use-case of conditional flow-matching: designing high-coverage predictive sets that cover the ground-truth regression target.

papers.summary: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) enables a language model to learn from a Teacher instantiated from the same model but given access to privileged information, such as a reference solution. papers.title: Why is AI-generated language so hard to understand?
papers.summary: There is a widespread sense that AI-generated text has recently become harder to understand. In this study, we investigate a set of psycholinguistic features that are known to correlate with human processing difficulty (e.g., object relative clauses, long syntactic dependencies, low-frequency n-grams). Using a novel corpus of AI-generated text across diverse domains, we find that AI models use these difficult features more often than paraphrases generated by round-trip translation. Compared with human writing, all nine frontier and near-frontier models use more inanimate subjects with animate verbs and more low-frequency n-grams, and most also use longer dependencies, more stacked nouns, and more reduced object relatives in conversation; we also demonstrate substantial variation across model families. We propose and test a hypothesis as to why: while human language is optimized for successful communication, AI-generated text is increasingly optimized for other goals like math, code, and reasoning, in which there is a pressure for \textit{information density} rather than successful communication. We provide a proof-of-concept for this hypothesis by fine-tuning a language model under a length penalty, which leads to a divergence from human-like linguistic behavior. Our findings highlight the axes of misalignment between linguistic processing demands in humans and LLMs, and point toward possible remedies.

papers.title: GRAFT: Restoring the Missing Sampling Interface in Continuous Diffusion Language Models
papers.summary: Continuous diffusion language models generate a whole sequence in parallel, never drawing a single word at any intermediate step; only the final step turns embeddings into text. We show that this same principle carries a hidden cost: a collapse of the lexical long tail. Measured against held-out human text, ELF's output matches the human rate on common words almost exactly, yet its rarest words appear at only 0.30x the human rate, a gap that does not close from 105M to 652M parameters and that no sampler setting these models expose can reach. A same-size GPT-2, in contrast, spans zero to above the human rate by its decoding rule alone. We trace the difference to what continuous diffusion models lack: with no step that ever draws a discrete word, every step is instead driven by an average over the candidates still in play, and averaging a rare candidate together with the common word competing for its slot lands on the common word. An autoregressive model avoids this because its decoding rule samples one candidate rather than averaging over all of them. We propose GRAFT, a training-free method that grafts this missing choice back onto a frozen model: while the model is still undecided, GRAFT commits the rare words the average would otherwise discard, then regenerates the sequence from scratch with those commitments held in place. papers.title: GRAM: Group-wise Rank-Aware Model Merging via Subspace Alignment
papers.summary: Merging different models into a single model is highly desirable for multi-task deployment, particularly in regulated domains like healthcare. papers.title: Deep Reasoning in General Purpose Agents via Structured Meta-Cognition

papers.title: Does Every Instance Count Equally? Order Effects in LLM Multi-Instance Processing
papers.summary: Users increasingly rely on large language models (LLMs) to analyse collections of independent inputs, such as product reviews or social media posts, and return a single aggregated answer. These results show that instance order can systematically bias aggregated predictions, highlighting the need to evaluate MIP across different input arrangements.

papers.title: GRAIL: From Saliency to Semantics in Time-Series Explanation
papers.summary: Explaining a time-series model requires both locating the evidence and extracting meaningful knowledge from it. Yet a single timestep is not a semantic unit: the meaningful patterns live across many samples, not in any one of them. Per-timestep saliency is therefore noisy, high-dimensional, and unstable. Existing methods address this by introducing fixed-size windows and treating them as independent players in a cooperative game. Evaluating a coalition of such players requires defining a ``baseline'' region, which prior work tackles with fixed counterfactuals (e.g., a flat line, noise, or a spectral surrogate). This choice frequently dominates the resulting explanation, obscuring the model's true decisions. To address these issues, we propose GRAIL, a region-based time-series explanation framework that uses domain-specific intervals, such as the P-wave and the QRS complex of an electrocardiogram (ECG) beat, as players. We describe each region with human-readable features and generate counterfactual baselines with an on-manifold conditional generator. Such a choice of players also admits non-temporal features: static covariates enter as singleton players attributed with the temporal regions on one scale, so a patient's tabular evidence (e.g., age, sex) is weighed directly against the signal. We attribute the predictions to the features via Owen values with common-random-number variance reduction. Experimental results on both synthetic and real data show that the proposed framework produces faithful and robust explanations, evaluated under matched on- and off-manifold operators, offering meaningful knowledge to domain experts.
