papers.title: Beyond the Teacher: Understanding and Preserving Distillation Overshoot in Agentic On-Policy Distillation
papers.summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains agents on their own trajectories using supervision from a stronger teacher. We uncover a counterintuitive phenomenon in multi-turn agentic tasks: a smaller, initially weaker student can substantially outperform its teacher during training, only to regress as distillation continues. We term this phenomenon distillation overshoot. Through decision- and task-level analyses, we trace overshoot to two competing effects of OPD: repairing weak student decisions and eroding successful student choices that the teacher disfavors. Early in training, repair outpaces erosion, allowing the student to combine the teacher's corrections with its own strengths and surpass the teacher. As training continues, erosion overtakes repair, causing these gains to vanish. Motivated by this finding, we propose Success-Preserving On-Policy Distillation (SPOD), which selectively masks conflicting teacher supervision on successful student choices and introduces a soft probability floor to counteract their erosion, while retaining teacher guidance elsewhere. SPOD requires only binary episode success and model probabilities already available during OPD. Across two model families and three agentic benchmarks, SPOD consistently outperforms ordinary OPD and evaluated variants, improving final success by up to 15.2 percentage points and surpassing the teacher by up to 20.0 points. Moreover, SPOD's final checkpoints outperform even ordinary OPD's best intermediate checkpoints in all six settings, demonstrating that beyond-teacher gains can be not only preserved but further extended. Code: https://github.com/Jike338/SPOD

papers.title: Refined Gradient-Based Temperature Optimization for the Replica-Exchange Monte-Carlo Method
papers.summary: The replica-exchange Monte-Carlo (RXMC) method is a powerful Markov-chain Monte-Carlo algorithm for sampling from multi-modal distributions, which are challenging for conventional methods. The sampling efficiency of the RXMC method depends highly on the selection of the temperatures, and finding optimal temperatures remains a challenge. In this study, we propose a refined online temperature selection method by extending the gradient-based optimization framework proposed previously. Building upon the existing temperature update approach, we introduce a reparameterization technique to strictly enforce physical constraints, such as the monotonic ordering of inverse temperatures, which were not explicitly addressed in the original formulation. The proposed method defines the variance of acceptance rates between adjacent replicas as a loss function, estimates its gradient using differential information from the sampling process, and optimizes the temperatures via gradient descent. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through experiments on benchmark spin systems, including the two-dimensional ferromagnetic Ising model, the two-dimensional ferromagnetic XY model, and the three-dimensional Edwards-Anderson model. Our results show that the method successfully achieves uniform acceptance rates and reduces round-trip times across the temperature space. Furthermore, our proposed method offers a significant advantage over recently proposed policy gradient method that require careful hyperparameter tuning, while simultaneously preventing the constraint violations that destabilize optimization.

papers.title: Human Responses to Algorithmic Correction: Evidence from Centre Court
papers.summary: We study how algorithmic review changes the initial decisions that a system is designed to correct. Using Hawk-Eye data from professional tennis, we compare umpire decisions with and without review against a common accuracy benchmark. Under review, initial errors were 8.6 percentage points higher just outside the line and lower for comparably close balls inside. We find no evidence that average initial accuracy deteriorated. Within matches, reversals were followed by larger adjustments than upheld calls, consistent with adaptation to correction. Overall, correction offsets worse initial decisions for incorrect in calls and reinforces better initial decisions for incorrect out calls. Whether review lowers organizational costs depends jointly on these changes and the costs of remedying corrected errors. A conditional illustration shows how utilization spreads fixed review costs across calls.

papers.title: SoK: PIAtlas: Decomposing the Unbounded Prompt Injection Attack Space
papers.summary: Prompt injection is the dominant security risk for large-language-model (LLM) applications and agents, yet the field still lacks a coherent map of how these attacks are constructed. More than twenty public datasets describe prompt injection using incompatible vocabularies, often organized around delivery vector, attacker goal, or generation method. In this Systematization of Knowledge, we present PIAtlas, a taxonomy organized instead around how the injected instruction is constructed to subvert the underlying model. Its six classes, one per subversion mechanism, form the roots of a hierarchy of techniques and sub-techniques that researchers can use to describe attacks consistently and design more systematic evaluations. We derive the taxonomy from how LLMs are trained, prompted, and influenced by human-like framing, and compare it with historical attack data. To ground this comparison, we release PICorpus, to our knowledge the largest license-clean collection of public prompt-injection datasets, and map thousands of its records to PIAtlas under a human-verified protocol. The mapping shows that attacks usually combine several techniques drawn from only a few mechanisms. It also reveals gaps that existing labels obscure: widely used agent benchmarks test only part of the attack space, and adaptive attackers favor mechanisms that curated benchmarks underrepresent. PIAtlas thus provides a common foundation for understanding this attack space, improving benchmark coverage, and guiding red teaming and defenses.

papers.title: Machine Learning for Coding Retail Product Names to Consumer-Price Categories: A Rule-plus-Bag-of-Words Pipeline with Reliability-Weighted Human-in-the-Loop Labeling
papers.summary: Price statistics increasingly draw on scanner, web-scraped and receipt data whose product names are short, noisy and carry no standard code, so they must be coded to consumption categories. A fine-tuned DistilBERT comes within half a point of the character model without passing it, at about 460 times its single-thread CPU inference cost. Character features reduce inference throughput 4.6-fold relative to unigram bag-of-words. A rule-based prefix-tree stage admits 75-86% of positive items, so in a cascade it bounds the recall of the whole pipeline. A Monte Carlo study of label aggregation with simulated annotators shows that an additive reliability weight barely improves on majority vote while Dawid-Skene aggregation recovers labels markedly better, and that this difference carries through to the character n-gram classifier. Sensitivity checks cover a planted shortcut, generator noise, training budget and annotator population. The benchmark is synthetic and English-language because the production data are under non-disclosure. Code, data and scripts are released; accuracies of models trained from scratch reproduce exactly, timings as ratios.

papers.title: DF-PALM: Dynamic Fusion Prompt Learning for Audio--Language Models
papers.summary: Few-shot audio classification requires audio--language models to distinguish variable acoustic events from limited labeled data. PALM's main formulation adapts encoded class representations without changing pretrained encoders, but its class representations remain input-independent and classification uses audio features without class-conditioned refinement. We introduce DF-PALM, a dynamic feature-space prompting framework that combines audio-conditioned class representations with asymmetric cross-attention for audio refinement. Class representations are conditioned after text encoding, held fixed across fusion layers for each input, and reused for final scoring. Both pretrained encoders remain frozen, avoiding audio-conditioned text-encoder passes. With PENGI as the frozen backbone, the main 16-shot evaluation covered 11 benchmarks and six baselines. DF-PALM achieved 80.69% mean accuracy and 80.32% macro-averaged F1, exceeding PALM by 4.11 and 4.30 percentage points, respectively. Paired benchmark-level tests supported both gains after Holm correction. Across four shot settings, DF-PALM achieved the highest mean accuracy and macro-averaged F1 among the four evaluated prompt-learning methods. The gains extended to LAION-CLAP and OpenFLAM, with significant improvements over PALM in both metrics. At 50 candidate classes, operator-counted inference floating-point operations increased by 0.39% relative to PALM. These results support instance-conditioned feature-space adaptation as an effective approach to few-shot audio classification. Our code is publicly available at GitHub https://github.com/sunyulin0421/DF-PALM.

papers.title: A Symmetry-Matching Approach to Blind-Spot Reduction in Sparse Autoencoders
papers.summary: Language models can treat semantically distinct inputs as interchangeable at the representation level, creating blind spots that standard sparse autoencoder (SAE) objectives do not target. In safety-critical settings such as clinical dosage extraction, legal clause interpretation, or financial amount verification, such failures can propagate silently into downstream decisions. We study this problem as one of feature-basis orientation. Building on a symmetry-matching view from algebraic error-detection theory, we add a differentiable $V_{\mathrm{Gini}}$ regularisation term to SAE training that penalises uneven perturbation response within a specified family. Across GPT-2, Gemma 2, and Qwen 2.5, a frozen multi-seed evaluation shows that $V$-regularisation raises both relative and absolute lower-tail responses while reducing response-profile imbalance, with no material general-text reconstruction degradation. JumpReLU and minimum description length (MDL) objectives remain close to the Standard SAE profile under the same protocol. Family-geometry controls show that the effect is not explained by template duplication or a single dominant perturbation family, and held-out probes plus null-calibrated separation tests evaluate how far the representation-level change carries to downstream discriminability. A zero-shot audit on out-of-distribution clinical radiology minimal pairs finds the relative weak-tail lift in all evaluated model-by-family cells, not perfectly rank-aligned with the trained statistic, and a held-out family audit finds it on family kinds never used in training. Together, the results show that perturbation-aware SAE training can reorient feature bases toward safety-relevant input changes while leaving downstream validation as a separate empirical step.

papers.title: How the Classical Baseline Shapes Machine-Learning Speed Claims in Topology Optimization
papers.summary: Topology optimization places material in a design domain to optimize a structure's performance, such as its stiffness or heat conduction. Machine-learning methods often report large speed-ups over classical, non-learned optimization, but a slow classical code or a lower-quality learned design can exaggerate them. We re-ran released code for eight methods on one workstation and studied two in depth: Optimize Any Topology (OAT), a diffusion model that generates designs, and a graph-based neural optimizer. Replacing the classical code with an efficient implementation of the same algorithm cut these two methods' speed-ups by up to 20-fold. We then timed the classical code until its design was at least as stiff as the learned one; for OAT, we picked this point after the runs, which gives the classical code its best case. Published timings imply a 134x speed-up for OAT on a 256 x 256 grid; our matched single-design comparisons gave 1.5x to 3.5x. At matched stiffness, the graph-based optimizer was slower than the classical code in all six two-dimensional problems. Of the six other methods, two kept their advantage, one shrank, one reversed, and two were not comparable. In an exploratory audit, language models judged that 8 of 28 speed comparisons in randomly sampled, openly accessible articles lacked evidence of equal design quality; our own review counted 11, so the count depends on who judges. We provide a comparison procedure and a minimum report: classical code, hardware, design quality, what each timing includes, and data-generation and training costs.

papers.title: Quantifying Memorization and Privacy Risks in Genomic Language Models
papers.summary: Genomic language models (GLMs) have emerged as powerful tools for learning representations of DNA sequences, enabling advances in variant prediction, regulatory element identification, and cross-task transfer learning. However, as these models are increasingly trained or fine-tuned on sensitive genomic cohorts, they risk memorizing specific sequences from their training data, raising serious concerns around privacy, data leakage, and regulatory compliance. Despite growing awareness of memorization risks in general-purpose language models, little systematic evaluation exists for these risks in the genomic domain, where data exhibit unique properties such as a fixed nucleotide alphabet, strong biological structure, and individual identifiability. We present a comprehensive, multi-vector privacy evaluation framework designed to quantify memorization risks in GLMs. Our approach integrates three complementary risk assessment methodologies: perplexity-based detection, canary sequence extraction, and membership inference. These are combined into a unified evaluation pipeline that produces a worst-case memorization risk score. To enable controlled evaluation, we plant canary sequences at varying repetition rates into both synthetic and real genomic datasets, allowing precise quantification of how repetition and training dynamics influence memorization. We evaluate our framework across multiple GLM architectures, examining the relationship between sequence repetition, model capacity, and memorization risk. Our results establish that GLMs exhibit measurable memorization and that the degree of memorization varies across architectures and training regimes. These findings reveal that no single attack vector captures the full scope of memorization risk, underscoring the need for multi-vector privacy auditing as a standard practice for genomic AI systems.

papers.title: Recurrent Temporal Restricted Boltzmann Machines as Unsupervised Encoders for Biomechanical Movement Sequences
papers.summary: Biomechanical movement recordings are continuous, high-dimensional time series, and analyzing them without manually labeling them requires representations that capture how movements evolve over time. papers.title: Compose the Horizon: Parameter-Shared Blockwise Forecasting under a Sequential-Compute Trade-off
papers.summary: Most long-horizon forecasters emit the complete future in one pass. We ask whether a compact operator can instead be reused to emit contiguous future blocks, trading stored parameters for sequential computation. Recursive Functional Decomposition (RFD) factorizes the horizon mapping into three parameter-shared block predictions. The blocks occupy disjoint future intervals and are concatenated, not added as trend, seasonal, or residual components, and each emitted block joins the rolling context that conditions the next application. In controlled three-seed experiments, removing forward feedback hurts all four evaluated datasets while stopping gradients through it changes little, so the useful signal is the evolving forecast state itself; reapplying the shared operator helps consistently, but by less than widening it. The model uses 0.08--0.46M parameters, yet its sequential channel-wise execution is slower and more memory-intensive than an iterative baseline at high channel count. papers.title: When Does Cheap Physics Help? Gated Multi-Fidelity Physics-Informed Networks with Provable Sample Savings and Conformal Guarantees

papers.title: FreshCast: Timely and Complementary Retrieval for Frozen Time Series Forecasters
papers.summary: Retrieval-augmented forecasting for Web and online services supplements a forecaster with the continuations of historical segments that resemble the current context. papers.title: Sparse Subspace-to-Expert Sharing for Task-Agnostic Continual Learning
papers.summary: Continual learning in Large Language Models (LLMs) is hindered by the plasticity-stability dilemma, where acquiring new capabilities often leads to catastrophic forgetting of previous knowledge. papers.title: Radial-Angular Geometry for Reliable Update Diagnosis in Noisy-Label Learning
papers.summary: Noisy-label methods often estimate sample reliability from forward-space signals such as loss, confidence, or entropy. These signals indicate whether a sample is difficult to predict, but they do not directly test whether its observed label induces a reliable parameter update. This gap matters because hard clean samples and mislabeled samples can have similar loss while inducing different updates. We recast reliability estimation as diagnosis of the observed-label update. The sample-wise empirical Fisher trace gives a backward-space measure of update energy: for the classifier layer, it factorizes into a prediction-residual term and a feature-sensitivity term, so it captures information beyond scalar loss. Trace, however, is still a radial magnitude signal and cannot decide whether a large update is useful or harmful. We therefore propose Relative Geometric Conflict (RGC), which compares the observed-label gradient with a reference gradient induced by an EMA teacher. The conflict term helps distinguish large but aligned hard-clean updates from large conflicting updates caused by corrupted labels. Across synthetic and real-world noisy-label benchmarks, RGC improves hard-clean preservation and accuracy under our evaluation protocol.

papers.title: What "Form'' of Uncertainty Does Conformal Prediction Quantify?
papers.summary: Conformal prediction (CP) is a post-hoc calibration method that returns prediction sets with distribution-free coverage guarantees, and the size of the output set is often interpreted as a notion of uncertainty. Essentially, this difference in set size is an aggregation of two opposite effects: (1) better model accuracy and therefore smaller set size achieved by training over extra calibration points, and (2) the "formability" of the model at test point towards every possible label. The latter effect vanishes with stronger models or more calibration data (as epistemic uncertainty is known for that behavior). It turns out that the model's formability itself (without the quantization effect of prediction sets, and through estimating the posterior variance) is a useful tool to quantify the epistemic uncertainty. papers.summary: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning improves the performance of Large Language Models (LLMs), yet it writes steps as text and follows one reasoning path at a time, which limits the capabilities of such models. Latent reasoning methods replace these steps with continuous thought representations and claim that a thought representation substitutes for the written reasoning, compresses trajectories, distinguishes semantic content, and achieves superposition of multiple exploration paths at once. These claims concern the content of the thought representation, whereas the evaluations of these methods rely on downstream task accuracy, token counts, and analyses specific to each method. We formalize these claims as a valid thought representation space and prove that a space is valid if and only if its thought representations attain four properties, namely causality, minimality, separability, and stability, each of which follows from one claim. Translating these properties into four measures and auditing three training-free and three trained methods shows gaps in these claims that accuracy may not necessarily reveal. Training-free methods fail all four properties and do not encode the reasoning they are meant to replace, whereas trained methods generally improve substitution. The four properties and measures therefore provide a theoretically grounded evaluation beyond downstream task accuracy and expose failure modes that may guide future development of latent reasoning methods.

papers.title: Can Agents Keep Secrets They Were Never Told? Benchmarking Latent Privacy Risks Across Sessions with MemJoin
papers.summary: To support sustained interactions and personalized assistance, agents use long-term memory to retain and combine user information across sessions. Reusing such memories can lead an agent to state a sensitive relation while completing an ordinary task that does not require it. The relation to protect and the combination of clues that reveal it may remain hidden at memory write time, when later records and tasks are still unknown. In this paper, we introduce MemJoin, a privacy benchmark of 288 synthetic analysis cases in which the complete history entails a sensitive relation, but every individual session is insufficient. We evaluate six memory systems with the same answer-generating model, alongside full-history and no-history controls. Each system writes and updates memories in session order and later retrieves context for an ordinary task, while target annotations remain with the evaluator. We separately check which target attribute values appear in stored records and retrieved context, and whether the final answer states the complete, person-linked relation. In a separate paired test on a prespecified subset, removing shared identifiers and other connecting clues can change complete-relation output while all checked target attribute values remain visible. These findings show why checking attribute visibility alone is insufficient to evaluate what records from different sessions reveal together.

papers.title: Task-aligned spectral inductive biases in parameterized quantum circuits
papers.summary: Parameterized quantum circuits are widely investigated in quantum machine learning, yet how their architecture can provide task-aligned inductive biases remains poorly understood. We study data reuploading quantum circuits with two distinct inputs: a signal that varies between samples and a fixed, task-defined spectral query that specifies how the signal should be probed. We examine this connection in a classification task inspired by synthetic aperture radar, where acquisition geometry determines a query for classifying unfocused spectral patches before image formation. Across small-scale spectral and radar-like tasks, aligned queries improve learning from limited data over parameter-matched circuits with mismatched or absent queries. papers.title: Diffusion-Based Stochastic Operator Networks for Uncertainty Quantification in Stochastic Partial Differential Equations
papers.summary: We introduce a novel framework for uncertainty quantification of solution operators associated with stochastic partial differential equations (SPDEs). Although SPDEs play a central role in modeling complex physical systems under uncertainty, their practical use typically requires specifying the magnitude and structure of model uncertainties that are often unknown and difficult to infer from noisy measurements. The proposed method, namely the Stochastic Operator Network (SON), is constructed by combining the structure of the Deep Operator Network (DeepONet) with Stochastic Neural Networks (SNNs) to model stochasticity and enable probabilistic prediction. The training procedure is carried out by minimizing a Hamiltonian-type loss and optimizing the resulting objective using the Stochastic Maximum Principle. papers.title: The Loss or the Architecture? What Matters in Survival Analysis with Competing Risks
papers.summary: Often, \emph{eg} in healthcare and predictive maintenance, what matters is which of several competing causes will strike first, and with what probability: survival analysis with competing risks. It brings twice as much as benefits a good choice of backbone on competing-risks data, and no more than it on single-event data: the loss is decisive for competing risks. The backbone matters too, and must match the modality: tabular networks lead on tables, pretrained vision encoders on images. The two choices compound rather than substitute. Proper scoring rules reveal these dynamics; the concordance index (C-index), which is not proper, does not separate models: neither axis moves it, not even tuning on the loss built to improve it. papers.title: Can the Parts Fool the Test? Counterfactual Pairing Cycles for Relational OOD
papers.summary: Relational out-of-distribution errors are easy to describe and hard to evaluate cleanly. An image may be natural, a caption may be fluent, and all mentioned objects may be common, yet the caption may describe the wrong relation in the image. papers.title: Phase Transition from Random Features to Fully Trainable Networks
papers.summary: Constructing accurate and computationally tractable approximation spaces is a fundamental task in scientific computing. papers.title: Reliable AI-Assisted Decisions via Selective Auditing

papers.title: A Fix for Softmax and Cross-Entropy
papers.summary: Standard implementations of softmax, log-softmax, and cross-entropy have two numerical bugs. The first bug, Softmax Collapse, rounds the target logit's gradient to zero if that one logit is much larger than the others, resulting in gradients that no longer sum to zero. The second bug, Softmax Cancellation, occurs when student logits are close to teacher logits, and produces non-zero gradients even when the student and teacher logits are equal. We present simple implementations of log-softmax, softmax, and cross-entropy that fix both bugs. papers.title: BeNice! Closing Looping's Inference-Memory Gap via KV-Sharing
papers.summary: Looped architectures scale quality while keeping parameter count fixed by repeatedly passing activations through the same block of layers. During inference, each recurrence generates independent KV-caches, causing memory to grow linearly. To address this challenge, prior work has proposed KV-sharing (i.e., sharing KV-caches across depth), finding that, in some cases, the KV-cache of the final recurrence can be shared with the earlier recurrences without quality loss, a property we denote as KV-shareability. However, the mechanisms underlying KV-shareability remain poorly understood, with even identically trained looped architectures not consistently exhibiting it. In this paper, we study how KV-shareability can be enabled in looped models. We propose a two-stage method: in the first stage, we use stochastic depth during pretraining, which induces contractive residual dynamics that drive representations toward a common limit across recurrences. In the second stage, we propose BeNice!, a post-training method that broadcasts the final recurrence's KV-cache into the first recurrence, training it to produce compatible residuals while preserving the original model's quality. As a result, BeNice! enables KV-shareability while matching standard finetuning's unshared validation perplexity. Using BeNice!, we show that KV-sharing is complementary to alternative KV-compression methods, composing with memory-efficient sequence mixers (e.g., multi-latent attention, Kimi delta attention) and low-precision KV-cache quantization (e.g., fp8, mxfp8, nvfp4). Finally, in simulated low-memory, long-context inference, KV-sharing improves cache hit rates by up to 31.4%, increases throughput by up to 23.6%, and reduces p90 time-to-first-token by up to 83.6%.

papers.title: OP-Print: Tracing Membership Imprints in On-Policy Self-Distillation

papers.title: Nonparametric autoregressive estimation of probability distributions with parallel gradient boosting

papers.title: Robust Tangent Space Estimation via Laplacian Eigenvector Gradient Orthogonalization
papers.summary: Estimating the tangent spaces of a data manifold is a fundamental problem in geometric data analysis. The standard approach, Local Principal Component Analysis (LPCA), struggles in high-noise settings due to a critical trade-off in choosing the neighborhood size. Selecting an optimal size requires prior knowledge of the geometric and noise characteristics of the data that are often unavailable. Instead of relying solely on local neighborhoods, LEGO estimates the tangent space at each data point by orthogonalizing the gradients of low-frequency eigenvectors of the graph Laplacian. We provide two theoretical justifications of our method. First, a differential geometric analysis on the tubular neighborhood of a manifold shows that gradients of the low-frequency Neumann eigenfunctions of the tube align closely with the manifold's tangent bundle, while an eigenfunction with high gradient in directions orthogonal to the manifold lies deeper in the spectrum. Second, a random matrix theoretic analysis also demonstrates that low-frequency eigenvectors are robust to sub-Gaussian noise. These results allow us to derive the asymptotic scaling and stability of the estimated eigenvector gradients. Numerical experiments demonstrate that LEGO yields tangent space estimates that are significantly more robust to noise than those from LPCA, resulting in marked improvements in downstream tasks such as manifold learning, boundary detection, and local intrinsic dimension estimation.

papers.title: Residual Correlation as a Diagnostic for Joint-Uncertainty Gains from GP Coregionalisation

papers.title: Giskard : Byzantine Robust and Private Aggregation for Large-Scale Decentralized Learning
papers.summary: In decentralized learning, clients train a machine learning model while keeping their data locally and share their model parameters or gradients with a set of neighbors, making it vulnerable to both privacy attacks and model poisoning attacks. Distributed DP can mitigate this issue by adding noise after aggregation, but implementing it without a trusted curator requires both confidential and Byzantine-resilient computation. However, these solutions scale badly: they either require all-to-all communication between participants or delegate the entire computation to a small subset of parties whose computational and communication cost grows with network size. In this paper, we present Giskard, a scalable protocol for private and Byzantine-robust decentralized aggregation. Giskard organizes $n$ parties into a tree of committees of size $O(\log n)$ and evaluates a differentially private coordinate-wise approximate median via a committee-adapted secure quantile search over the value domain, using MPC within each committee. We assess Giskard both theoretically by proving its security and privacy properties and empirically through extensive experiments involving up to one million participants. Compared to its closest competitors, Giskard reduces per-party communication complexity by close to three orders of magnitude over the closest competitor while exhibiting comparable robustness under up to $n/4$ Byzantine parties.

papers.title: The Bayesian Learning Rule Beyond KL Geometry

papers.title: Poisoning-Based Backdoors Are Not Cryptographic
papers.summary: Defending against a backdoor requires recovering the verifier that decides whether an input is a trigger, since blocking individual triggers fails against an attacker who can generate new ones. If a verifier could be installed with the asymmetry of cryptographic authentication, where only the attacker can produce triggers and the defender cannot reconstruct the verifier, defense that learns the verifier from observations would be impossible in principle. We show that no such asymmetry can arise when the verifier enters training only through the labels of poisoned data, which covers the dirty-label backdoors that dominate the literature on language models. A training procedure that installs a verifier from poisoned data is itself a learner for that verifier. Hence any verifier that is hard to learn cannot be installed through poisoning, and any verifier that poisoning can install is reconstructible by a white-box defender holding as many labeled trigger observations as the attacker used. Hiding a secret key in the input or the weights does not change this. Experiments on instruction-tuned large language models confirm the dichotomy, with no configuration yielding a backdoor that is both effective for the attacker and irrecoverable for the defender.

papers.title: Efficient Adjoint Matching for Fine-tuning Diffusion Models
papers.summary: Reward fine-tuning has become a common approach for aligning pretrained diffusion and flow models with human preferences in text-to-image generation. However, AM inevitably requires a substantial computational cost: it requires (i) stochastic simulation of full generative trajectories under memoryless dynamics, resulting in a large number of function evaluations, and (ii) backward ODE simulation of the adjoint state along each sampled trajectory. In this work, we observe that both bottlenecks are closely tied to the non-trivial base drift inherited from the pretrained model. Motivated by this observation, we propose Efficient Adjoint Matching (EAM), which substantially improves training efficiency by reformulating the SOC problem with a linear base drift and a correspondingly modified terminal cost. This reformulation removes both sources of inefficiency; it enables training-time sampling with a few-step deterministic ODE solver and yields a closed-form adjoint solution that eliminates backward adjoint simulation. On standard text-to-image reward fine-tuning benchmarks, EAM converges up to 4x faster than AM and matches or surpasses it across various metrics including PickScore, ImageReward, HPSv2.1, CLIPScore and Aesthetics.

papers.title: Diagnostic Loss: Asymmetric Supervision for Radiology Report Generation
papers.summary: Automated radiology report generation requires models to do more than produce fluent clinical narratives: they must explicitly state supported diagnoses while avoiding unsupported ones. However, existing medical vision-language models (MedVLMs) are typically trained with token-level maximum likelihood objectives, which prioritize text agreement over diagnostically critical terms. Across these settings, DLoss improves diagnostic faithfulness while maintaining competitive performance on conventional language-generation metrics, showing the value of asymmetric sequence-level supervision for radiology report generation. papers.title: Tracing Subliminal Learning Through Pretraining
papers.summary: Large language models trained on data generated by other models can sometimes inherit traits unrelated to that data, a phenomenon called subliminal learning. In our experiments, soft label distillation produces more consistent transfer with less extensive training than hard label distillation. papers.title: One Teacher, Many Views: Reducing Reference Sensitivity in On-Policy Self-Distillation
papers.summary: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) improves reasoning by training a model on its own trajectories with dense token-level supervision from a privileged copy conditioned on a reference solution. Although it provides evidence about the answer, it also encodes an ordering, phrasing, and solution path. Full-reference conditioning can therefore produce correct targets that depend excessively on information unavailable to the student at inference. We show that this probability-space average is the exact target induced by minimizing the expected teacher-to-student KL divergence over privileged views. papers.title: Joules-to-GDP: How Much Economic Value Do AI Systems Produce per Unit of Energy?
papers.summary: An AI system can produce more economically valuable work while delivering less value for the energy it consumes. papers.title: Reverse-KL Policy Distillation: Statistical Guarantees and Limits
papers.summary: Reverse Kullback-Leibler (KL) distillation has shown empirical promise for training language models, but its statistical guarantees and limits remain poorly understood. These statistical guarantees do not follow simply from optimizing standard distillation objectives: our lower bounds show that common online objectives can fail when candidates are evaluated only on past student-generated trajectories. papers.title: Tractable Inference with Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks
papers.summary: Machine-learning surrogates in computational science often require not only accurate predictions but also expectations, variances, conserved integrals, and normalization constants. Under factorizing input measures, expectations and higher moments then reduce algebraically to deterministic recursions over one-dimensional leaf integrals. Independent and shared inner-block variants form a parameter-efficiency hierarchy, and a universal-approximation proof for its most restricted member extends to the complete class. The same deterministic operators allow conserved integrals and normalization to be imposed throughout training. Across uniform and Gaussian benchmarks through 50 dimensions, deterministic mean and variance errors remained below the median fixed-budget Monte Carlo errors in every case. TOUCKANs also conserved Cahn--Hilliard mass to machine precision and imposed normalization and orthogonality through deterministic moments, enabling joint computation of the lowest four Schrödinger eigenpairs in two, three, and five dimensions. TOUCKANs therefore connect KAN approximation with tractable probabilistic circuits, making statistical operators and integral constraints directly available within an expressive neural surrogate.

papers.title: Towards Faithful Data Selection: Statistical Limits and Scalable Algorithms
papers.summary: What does it mean to have an optimal data selection algorithm? papers.title: From Classifier Heads to Encoder Prototypes: Personalized Federated Learning with Head-Derived Clustering

papers.title: Looped Uniform Diffusion Language Models
papers.summary: Uniform diffusion language models (UDLMs) generate text by iteratively denoising sequences of ordinary vocabulary tokens, any of which may be corrupted and subsequently revised. papers.title: The Limits of Post-Selection Generalization
papers.summary: While statistics and machine learning offer numerous methods for ensuring generalization, these methods often fail in the presence of adaptivity---the common practice in which the choice of analysis depends on previous interactions with the same dataset. A recent line of work has introduced powerful, general purpose algorithms that ensure post hoc generalization (also called robust or post-selection generalization), which says that, given the output of the algorithm, it is hard to find any statistic for which the data differs significantly from the population it came from. In this work we show several limitations on the power of algorithms satisfying post hoc generalization. First, we show a tight lower bound on the error of any algorithm that satisfies post hoc generalization and answers adaptively chosen statistical queries, showing a strong barrier to progress in post selection data analysis. Second, we show that post hoc generalization is not closed under composition, despite many examples of such algorithms exhibiting strong composition properties.

papers.title: Privacy Accounting for Empirical Denoisers
papers.summary: Diffusion models have emerged as the foundation of modern generative systems, yet their high memorization capacity raises privacy concerns. While differentially private (DP) training provides formal guarantees, it comes at a cost in sample quality. In this work, we study a complementary question: how much privacy loss is incurred during the sampling process itself? Directly analyzing modern neural denoisers is challenging because their sensitivity to a single training example is generally intractable. To overcome this challenge, we construct and analyze a clipped privacy-accountable empirical denoiser, a training-free estimator of the Bayes-optimal denoiser, whose per-step sensitivity can be computed explicitly, allowing each denoising step to be a Gaussian mechanism. This perspective enables privacy accounting under Gaussian DP when each training example contributes to each denoising step, and under $f$-DP trade-off functions when each generated sample uses a single randomly subsampled block of the training data. We report every $(\varepsilon, δ)$ guarantee as a certified upper bound from a privacy loss distribution accountant, and use a cumulant-based Edgeworth approximation as a fast diagnostic, characterizing where it is reliable and where it becomes anti-conservative. We also analyze the privacy loss along the denoising trajectory and show that it grows steeply near the critical window in which semantic content is formed. This observation motivates hybrid samplers that use the private empirical denoiser through the formative steps where it remains a faithful proxy for the neural denoiser, then switch to a public neural denoiser for the remaining refinement. Our results on CIFAR-10 and CelebA-64 show that the privacy of diffusion models depends not only on the training procedure, but also on sampling-time design choices such as subsampling, stopping time, and hybrid denoising.

papers.title: Mitigating Model Collapse through Dreaming Learning
papers.summary: Training generative models on synthetic data causes loss of diversity and a decrease in performance, a phenomenon known as model collapse. We study this degeneration spectrally in a controlled Markov setting. The eigenvalue spectrum of the learned transition operator offers a direct view of the process, since the subdominant eigenvalues set how fast the chain mixes and therefore how much of the state space it continues to explore. We find that sampling at temperature $T_s < 1$ acts on the operator like repeated sharpening, pushing it toward a deterministic system: the subdominant eigenvalues approach the unit circle and the spectral gap narrows. When $T_s < 1$, even data accumulation does not appear to arrest this drift. We then analyze Dreaming Learning, a regulariser that, in parallel with regular training, adds a loss term on the model's own samples drawn at a raised temperature $T_d > 1$. Because high-temperature samples flatten the predicted distribution, training on them keeps the entries of the learned operator from becoming vanishingly small, which in turn keeps the eigenvalues bounded away from the unit circle. Measurements of the spectra over 5000 generations are consistent with this picture, and the mitigation effect persists in more complex settings such as LSTM language models and a 124M-parameter GPT-2.

papers.title: Language Modeling with Hyperspherical Flows

papers.title: The Price of Current-Effect Inference in Nonstationary Multi-Armed Bandits
papers.summary: Adaptive experiments use bandit algorithms to favor interventions with higher expected rewards. papers.title: Fixed Sets and the Hardness of Computing Correlated Equilibria

papers.title: Phase Transitions in Learning Driven by Extremal Data

When the max pooling model is the true data generating process, learning will be successful when $λ$ is increased during gradient descent, thereby driving the dynamics into regions of parameter space with vanishing gradients. To understand the conditions under which gradient descent breaks down, we study a minimal model and derive a low dimensional projection of the gradient flow in the joint limit of large bags $n$ and high dimension $d$ with $α=\ln n/d$ fixed. The flow has two distinct phase transitions: an intrinsic freezing transition related to the random energy model of disordered systems, and a retrieval transition occurring in modern Hopfield networks. papers.title: Euclidean Fourier Neural Operators
papers.summary: Fourier neural operators (FNOs) provide an efficient framework for learning mappings between function spaces as they are, by construction, independent of the grid resolution at which they are trained and evaluated. papers.title: GaP-MoE : Explicit Expert Specialization in Mixture-of-Experts via Orthogonal Gradient Accumulation and Projection
papers.summary: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (SMoE) models improve scalability by routing input tokens to only a subset of expert networks, but they often suffer from representation collapse, in which multiple experts converge toward similar functions and lose their intended diversity. papers.title: Reader--Writer Coupling in Transformer MLPs
papers.summary: A transformer MLP gives each hidden channel two roles: a reader that decides when the channel responds, and a writer that decides what it adds back to the residual stream. Read as a key--value memory, the layer can be measured one factor set at a time: the pairing of readers to writers is carried only by their shared index, invisible to any quantity computed from one factor set alone. Yet training couples the two factors through their joint update, so we ask what reading them together shows. The block supplies the joint instrument: the MLP writes back into the very stream it reads, so the exact Jacobian of its update is square, and its agreement with its own transpose resolves into reader--writer terms whose inner products give each channel, read as a couple, a signed pairing coordinate. Ranked by this coordinate, each block we measure has a small core of strongly coupled channels; where initialization gives either sign equally, the core is nearly all opposed: each writer points against the direction its reader responds to. This opposed core recurs from the smallest models trained from scratch to released checkpoints; its sign is in place within a few percent of training and holds while the coupling grows. Read as couples, most channels return their contribution against the reader that fired it, and the readers of later blocks take it up; few show in the logits. Training holds the couples in place: flipping the opposed writers moves the output toward common tokens, and a writer permuted onto another reader regrows to fit that reader while the reader stays.

papers.title: Approximate Solomonoff Induction: On the Robustness of Learned Universal Predictors
papers.summary: Why large language models trained via log-loss minimization over massive and diverse datasets exhibit broad capabilities and generalizable skills is not yet fully understood. Grau-Moya et al. (ICML 2024) offer a conceptual explanation through the lens of meta-learning: if sequence-generating environments $ν$ are drawn from a prior $w_ν$, minimizing population log-loss recovers the corresponding Bayesian mixture predictor $ξ=\sum_νw_νν$. In the idealized limit in which $w$ is a universal prior, the optimal predictor corresponds to Solomonoff universal induction. Practical machine learning algorithms, however, generally produce only \emph{approximately} optimal predictors. This raises a natural question: \emph{Does the prediction performance remain robust under approximation}? In this paper, we first provide a tight bound on the worst-case effect of approximation on prediction error. We show any predictor $ρ$ satisfying $D_{KL}(ξ\|ρ)\leq η$ retains bounded cumulative-expected-squared prediction error. However, while the Bayesian mixture predictor $ξ$ has error $O(\log(1/w_μ))$ in an environment $μ$, we establish a tight $Θ(η/w_μ)$ bound on the excess error of $ρ$ relative to $ξ$. Thus, approximation can substantially degrade performance in environments assigned small prior probability. In sharp contrast, when environments are averaged according to prior $w$, we prove that the excess prediction error is only $O(η)$. Furthermore, we establish a distribution-shift theorem for dominated shifts from a training prior $w$ to a test prior $w'$, interpolating our average-case and worst-case guarantees. Finally, we extend our robustness analysis to a finite-sampling setting relevant to learning universal predictors with neural networks and Transformers, where $D_{KL}(ξ\|ρ)$ could be unbounded. papers.title: Compression Through Time: An Interplay of Separability, Stationarity and Capacity
papers.summary: Information-theoretic and geometric compression have been widely studied as possible explanations for generalization. Yet their temporal dynamics in recurrent networks remain largely unexplored. Using discretized LSTMs, whose finite embedding space enables direct estimates of information quantities, we observe pronounced compression across the final timesteps of many datasets. We explain this effect through three competing mechanisms: (i) class separability permits stronger compression at the final timestep; (ii) shared recurrent dynamics propagate this pressure across timesteps with similar activation states, making its extent depend on temporal stationarity; and (iii) limited representational capacity opposes prolonged compression because it restricts information available for subsequent computation. We systematically test these mechanisms through controlled synthetic interventions and real-world sequence tasks. Our results identify class separability, temporal stationarity, and network capacity as key determinants of temporal compression, and suggest that compression acts as a regularizer-potentially beneficial when excess capacity is available, but harmful to generalization when it consumes memory needed for the task.

papers.title: DriftNeRF: Cross-Ray Density Drifting for Sparse-View Neural Radiance Fields
papers.summary: Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) synthesize photorealistic novel views from dense image collections, but degrade sharply when few views are available. We make this quantity explicit by measuring cross-ray density disagreement directly during training, and show that it stays high in vanilla NeRF, falls only incidentally under frequency-based regularization, and moves together with held-out quality in the sparse regime. The regularizer reads only sampled positions, ray identifiers, and predicted densities, so it requires no pretrained model, external geometry, or additional images, and transfers across field parameterizations. papers.title: Lower Bounds for Smooth Nonconvex Zeroth-Order Optimization: The Price of Determinism under Low Curvature Trace

papers.title: Copying Under Repetition: From Prefix Matching to Position Hashing

papers.title: When Weak Submodularity Meets Matroids: How Does Standard Greedy Behave?

papers.title: Small-Scale Experiments: Are We There Yet?
papers.summary: Scaling laws promised cost-effective experiments; six years later, they have yet to fully deliver. Instead, researchers have found them unreliable at small scales (starting at 4M parameters) and concluded that sizable models cannot be avoided. We show this is not the case: the confounding factor is hyperparameters. Small models are highly sensitive, but hyperparameter sensitivity fades with scale. This small-scale sensitivity makes scaling laws easy to miss because they only emerge on the fully tuned frontier, and reaching that frontier requires an extensive search far beyond what most ever run. By ablating the basic scaling law recipe, we show well-tuned hyperparameters matter more than any other ingredient. Further, we reveal why those hyperparameters become easier to find: as scale increases, the hyperparameter loss surface becomes lower dimensional. Nevertheless while scaling laws exist in small models, extrapolation hits statistical limitations. A holistic approach is required. Synthesizing our insights with the recent literature, we develop a new methodology for model-centric research and demonstrate it on a question that once took the field years to settle: where to place normalization layers in the transformer architecture. From small-scale experiments, we recover the large scale result: pre-normalization works better as models grow in size. With the right tools and a better understanding, small-scale experiments can deliver on scaling laws' long-awaited promise.

papers.title: How Does Orthogonalization Adapt to the Neural Network Hessian Structure? A Gradient Self Outer-Product Analysis at Initialization

Diagonal dominance of $\mathbf{V}\mathbf{V}^\top$ has been observed in language models, but why a neural network produces it has not been explained. In theoretical models, a single linear map that reads back every combination of nonzero features needs a width nearly quadratic in their number, while sparse optimization can succeed with a width linear in that number. In practice, one may hope to interpret a trained network by recovering its features in the same way. However, its features are usually unknown, and thus they are estimated from its activations or weights by recovery methods, such as sparse autoencoders and transcoders. In this work, we organize the theory of superposition by the decoder class and its practice by the strength of the claims about a feature supported by each method's results. On the theory side, we review the lower bounds on the overlap between feature directions, the conditions under which trained toy models share dimensions among features, and the separation between storing features and computing new features. On the practice side, we categorize recovery methods into four families, from probes for a named feature to decompositions of the trained weights. We then compare their evaluations, failure modes, and applications, and grade the evidence on one scale of claims about a feature. Finally, we assess previously stated open problems and identify remaining theoretical and empirical questions about superposition in trained networks. papers.title: When Retain Constraints Conflict: Mitigating Forget-Retain Interference in Tabular Data
papers.summary: Machine unlearning aims to remove the influence of designated training data while preserving model utility, but its behavior on tabular data remains underexplored. papers.title: Combating Catastrophic Forgetting in Continual Domain Adaptation via Knowledge Recasting
papers.summary: Adapting language models to new domains during post-training risks degrading previously acquired capabilities, a phenomenon commonly known as catastrophic forgetting. papers.title: A Reverse-Gold Theorem: Positive-Data Identification by Substrate-Bounded Contrastive Learners
papers.summary: Gold's theorem shows that no learner can identify an arbitrary language in a superfinite class from positive presentations alone. We prove a positive result of a different shape. The negatives are constructed by the learner, not supplied by an oracle, and no global normalizing constant over strings is ever computed. The misranking bound follows from the geometry of the contrastive loss---per-example loss floors plus a definite loss increment under misranking---yielding an $\varepsilon^{-2}$ rate, together with an explicit approximation gap that quantifies the cost of in-language (``colliding'') perturbations and vanishes for orbit-pure operators. papers.title: Do Neural Models Prefer Their Submodels?

papers.title: Beyond the Point Mass: Acceptance-Derived Weights and Distributional Losses for Speculative Decoding
papers.summary: In speculative decoding, a lightweight draft model proposes tokens that the target model verifies in parallel, speeding up generation without changing the target distribution. papers.title: A Simple and General Approach to top-$k$ Selection

papers.title: AURA: Angular Update Rate Adaptation for training complex-valued neural networks
papers.summary: Complex-valued neural networks (CVNNs) are increasingly adopted for complex-valued data; however, they are often trained with first-order optimizers inherited from the real-valued case. It requires no additional gradient evaluations and only inexpensive vector operations per step. Fully connected neural networks are used throughout this work. papers.title: Predicting silent failures of learned inference under restricted access: what measurement physics and prior information explain
papers.summary: Learned priors are used to reconstruct regions that measurements barely reach, and to report uncertainty there. They can fail silently: the reported interval excludes the truth while every ground-truth-free diagnostic stays within its noise. We call such errors the blind set and ask whether they can be predicted before the target data are seen. For a correctly specified linear-Gaussian model averaged over the prior, the risk of a silent failure factorises exactly into non-detection and non-coverage, which does not hold for learned systems in general; we build a score that approximates this reference by linearising a VAE prior. In a prospective study on real X-ray CT objects (2DeteCT) under simulated restricted access, with predictions committed by hash before any trial, the score ranked the realised blindness of two learned inference systems (latent Laplace and ensemble Kalman inversion) with Spearman $ρ= 0.79$ and 0.84 over 240 pre-specified errors. Simple structural predictors would also have passed these tests. Sequential post-hoc analyses, each specified before its own computation, show that under bounded reach the learned score gave no detectable improvement over a physics-based baseline, in rankings or trial-level log scores. At the weakest attenuation studied, prior information improved rankings over the physics-based baseline, most clearly for ensemble Kalman inversion, but a Gaussian prior did as well and the gain was not detectable at the trial level. The score is not a calibrated probability. Silent failures can be anticipated here, but their structure follows mainly from measurement access and the decision quantity rather than from the learned prior.

papers.title: Scalable Stress-Constrained Topology Optimization: A Super-resolution and Simultaneous Approach Based on Machine Learning
papers.summary: Large-scale topology optimization (TO) remains computationally demanding, especially for stress-constrained problems. This optimization minimizes a multi-component loss function that combines the design objective, an aggregation of the local stress constraints, and the potential energy functionals. Our NNs have a unique architecture that accelerates convergence while enabling the networks to capture sharp gradients and boundaries which are critical to stress-constrained TO. Unlike domain decomposition approaches, our partitioning naturally ensures field continuity across the subdomains and does not require the introduction of additional terms into the loss function. papers.title: When Does Training on Synthetic Data Provably Work?
papers.summary: High-quality training data are a major bottleneck in machine learning, motivating increasing use of artificially generated data. papers.title: FEAST: Federated Shared-Space Training for Resource-Heterogeneous Clients

papers.title: QML-PipeGuard: Detecting Channel-Substitution Attacks on Quantum Machine Learning Pipelines in Untrusted Clouds
papers.summary: As machine-learning workloads move onto quantum hardware they inherit a trust problem classical AI deployments have largely solved and quantum ones have not: quantum machine learning (QML) is already sold as a cloud service, and a customer cannot check that the circuit they paid for is actually the circuit that ran. A malicious or cost-cutting provider can substitute the declared quantum channel with one that reproduces every accuracy test the customer performs, passes the single-observable checks used in practice, and still differs from the declared computation at the channel level. QML-PipeGuard detects the attack at runtime from measurement statistics the customer already collects. Its guarantee is two-sided, stated in the distance a local verifier measures: any substitution shifting a single-qubit output marginal by $δ$ in trace norm forces a contract deviation of at least $δ/\sqrt{3}$, the constant tight and independent of qubit count; the guarantee is relative to the chosen observable family and reference-input set. For local-unitary substitutions the adversary's blind set is characterised exactly, as a commutation condition, which gives the defender a rule for choosing challenge inputs that shrinks it. A finite-shot budget rule bounds false accepts and false alarms at once, one tolerance separates attack from the benign drift observed here, and every decision enters a hash-anchored audit trail. On an IBM Heron r2 processor a substituted quantum-kernel intrusion-detection pipeline evades the weak contract and our verifier halts it, while the honest channel stays within tolerance.

papers.title: Beyond Invariance: Factor-wise Selective Treatment of Shifts for Multimodal Learning

papers.title: Federated Learning: From Theory to Practice
papers.summary: This book offers a hands-on introduction to building and understanding federated learning (FL) systems. FL enables multiple devices -- such as smartphones, sensors, or local computers -- to collaboratively train machine learning (ML) models, while keeping their data private and local. The book is designed for students, engineers, and researchers who want to learn how to design scalable, privacy preserving FL systems. Our main focus is on personalization: enabling each device to train its own model while still benefiting from collaboration with relevant devices. This is achieved by leveraging similarities between (the learning tasks associated with) devices that are encoded by the weighted edges (or links) of a federated learning network (FL network). The key idea is to represent real-world FL systems as networks of devices, where nodes correspond to device and edges represent communication links and data similarities between them. The training of personalized models for these devices can be naturally framed as a distributed optimization problem. This optimization problem is referred to as generalized total variation minimization (GTVMin) and ensures that devices with similar learning tasks learn similar model parameters. Our approach is both mathematically principled and practically motivated. While we introduce some advanced ideas from optimization theory and graph-based learning, we aim to keep the book accessible. papers.title: Some remarks on the connection between generative diffusion and optimal transport
papers.summary: We discuss three simple connections between generative diffusion and optimal transport. First, the joint law of the data and of their Ornstein-Uhlenbeck noising is, at every time, the solution of an entropic optimal-transport problem, at a temperature set by the noise level. Backward diffusion can consequently be read as an annealing which gradually decreases the entropic regularization. Second, we study the speciation transition--how the modes of the data distribution emerge during generation--and compare how it happens in diffusion and flow matching with respect to optimal transport. Using Gaussian mixtures as high-dimensional example, we show that the dynamical instability through which diffusion and flow matching separate the modes becomes, for optimal transport, an exponentially thin boundary layer at the beginning of generation, which is rounded by entropic regularization. Third, considering a generic forward dynamics with a general confining potential, we show that the backward process driven by the score also satisfies a drift-based variational principle whose minimal cost is the entropy difference between initial and final distributions.

papers.title: From Generic to Dedicated: A Novel Optimizer for Online Continual Learning

papers.title: Influence Is the Target-Response Jacobian Times Residuals
papers.summary: We introduce the target-response Jacobian $J = [\partial \hat y_i/\partial y_j]$, which measures how model predictions respond to changes in individual training targets. $J$ complements training-data attribution (TDA) methods, which characterize sensitivity to the weights placed on training observations in the loss rather than to their targets, and can be computed matrix-free at the same cost as influence-based TDA methods. For canonical-link losses (squared error, logistic, Poisson) the multiplier is the training residual, $\mathcal{I} = J\operatorname{diag}(r)$, and softmax cross-entropy obeys a multiclass version. The identity predicts three ways in which influence fails when used in place of $J$: small residuals shrink its predicted shift towards zero (interpolation collapse), residuals of mixed sign wash out its direction (direction washout), and under softmax cross-entropy it collapses a training point's per-class sensitivities towards its own true class (true-class collapse). papers.title: Double-Diffusion: Balancing Speed, Accuracy, and Uncertainty in Probabilistic Forecasting for Urban Sensor Networks

papers.title: Fixed-Size Active Statistical Inference

papers.title: Complete or Sparse: A Tale of Two Identifiabilities

papers.title: Physics-Inspired Optimizers beyond the Edge of Stability: Period-Two Orbits and Delayed Instability
papers.summary: Gradient descent with momentum can be viewed as a particle moving with friction in the loss landscape. In deep learning the learning rate is usually large, so training is a discrete dynamical system: in many full-batch experiments the sharpness grows to the optimizer's stability limit, the edge of stability (EoS), and training continues there. Physics-inspired optimizers change this motion; Velocity-Regularized Adam (VRAdam), for example, shrinks the step at high speed. We study kinetic maps, in which the step is the gradient of a kinetic energy of the momentum, and ask what they do beyond the EoS. (i) In a reduced model, a kinetic map creates a symmetric period-two orbit beyond the edge, strictly linearly stable if and only if the map's elasticity (the log-log slope of step length versus momentum) lies between 0 and 1; on it, training sits at an effective edge of stability. VRAdam's damper fails above twice the critical learning rate, where its kinetic energy is not convex; the Legendre dual of VRAdam's own Lagrangian is convex and passes at every learning rate. (ii) Because the sharpness rises gradually, the loss of stability is delayed, as in Neishtadt's theory of slowly swept bifurcations. In a network with a controlled sweep, the dynamics match this theory without fitted parameters, including the memory of where the sweep started and its erasure by noise. (iii) With momentum, reaching the oscillation also requires elasticity at large momentum: maps that bound the step have competing period-four and chaotic attractors already at beta1 = 0.9, while the cubic-Legendre map reached the oscillation from every sampled start up to beta1 = 0.99. papers.title: CAVA: Complementary-Label-Aware Data Valuation
papers.summary: Complementary-label learning (CLL) trains a classifier from labels that name a class an instance does not belong to. The transferred score is informative only at sufficiently high noise, becomes uninformative at the crossover rate $1/M$ for $M$ classes, and reverses below it, where practical CLL annotation typically operates. We propose CAVA, which introduces a complementary label cost and a label margin that isolates the contribution of each complementary label to the transport potential. On synthetic and human-annotated benchmarks, CAVA separates diagonal noise almost perfectly where directly transferred OT valuation performs worse than random. papers.title: Cross-Fitting for Neural Posterior Estimation
papers.summary: Neural Posterior Estimation (NPE) fits an amortized conditional density estimator to a simulated training set of complete-data realizations. Early stopping and other regularizers can prevent this degeneracy, but they are limited to selecting posterior approximations along an unfavorable optimization trajectory set by in-sample residuals, where the posterior mean is underfit while the posterior variance is overfit. Using $K$-fold cross-fitting, CF-NPE fits $K$ posterior-mean regressors and then fits a conditional density estimator to the resulting out-of-fold residuals. papers.title: Risk-averse learning with delayed feedback
papers.summary: In real-world scenarios, risk-averse learning is valuable for mitigating potential adverse outcomes. However, the delayed feedback makes it challenging to assess and manage risk effectively. In this paper, we investigate risk-averse learning using Conditional Value at Risk (CVaR) as risk measure, while incorporating feedback with random but bounded delays. We develop two risk-averse learning algorithms that rely on one-point and two-point zeroth-order optimization approaches, respectively. The dynamic regrets of the algorithms are analyzed in terms of the cumulative delay and the number of total samplings. In the absence of delay, the regret bounds match the established bounds of zeroth-order stochastic gradient methods for risk-averse learning. Furthermore, the two-point risk-averse learning outperforms the one-point algorithm by achieving a smaller regret bound. We provide numerical experiments on a dynamic pricing problem to demonstrate the performance of the algorithms.

papers.title: User Model Extraction via Belief Self-Distillation
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) implicitly infer attributes of their users and adapt their behavior accordingly, yet these beliefs remain difficult to inspect and causally manipulate. We introduce Belief Self-Distillation (BSD), a unified read-write framework that bridges linear and causal probing by learning a compact user representation that can be both decoded and written back into the model. The frozen LLM acts as its own teacher, distilling beliefs from natural conversations without external annotations. Unlike conventional probing, BSD isolates not only information present in activations, but a state whose causal role can be directly tested. Across multiple model families, BSD faithfully recovers user beliefs and enables substantially stronger interventions than matched hidden-state steering. Crucially, we find that refusal depends not only on the request, but on the model's inferred user intent: changing this belief alters refusal while holding the request fixed. We further uncover a striking cross-model regularity: independently trained LLMs converge on a shared geometry for representing their users. Together, these results reveal implicit user models as readable and causally writable internal states with direct implications for AI safety, shaping how models condition safety decisions on whom they believe they are interacting with.

papers.title: Residual Stochastic Concept Bottleneck Models
papers.summary: Concept-based models (CMs) learn human-interpretable intermediate representations that enable users to understand the model's reasoning and steer its predictions through test-time concept interventions. However, in realistic settings, their performance can be limited by concept incompleteness, where the training concepts fail to capture all task-relevant information. Adding an unconstrained residual pathway to the model's predictive process can overcome the consequences of incompleteness. However, this introduces an inscrutable, leak-prone prediction pathway that may weaken concept interventions, as these often leave residual variables unchanged. To address this limitation, we introduce Residual Stochastic Concept Bottleneck Models (Res-SCBMs), a family of concept-based models that jointly model concept and residual variables through a multivariate Gaussian distribution. Res-SCBMs learn a covariance structure that explicitly captures dependencies between the known concepts and learnt residual variables, allowing interventions to propagate to statistically dependent residual variables through Gaussian conditioning. This extends the intervention capabilities of previous CMs without requiring concept completeness during training. Our results show that, across multiple concept-incomplete benchmarks, Res-SCBMs improve predictive performance over competing baselines while retaining effective test-time concept interventions.

papers.title: Strength Controls Change How Interventions Compare Across Sparse Autoencoder Codes
papers.summary: Changing sparse autoencoder (SAE) codes can alter both intervention direction and magnitude, so comparing intervention effects requires a strength control specifying what is held equal. Norm matching and output calibration provide different controls, but whether interventions yield different effects across codes after strength matching remains unclear. We compare intervention effects under these controls for fixed feature groups in Gemma and Llama and observe: (1) Whole-patch scaling. With one coefficient per input, full-output Kullback-Leibler (KL) calibration leaves smaller mean effect gaps from the encoder-based reference intervention than total-norm matching for nonnegative least-squares (NNLS) refits. On new Llama inputs, total-norm matching loses 11 reference transfers, whereas full-output calibration preserves every transfer decision. (2) Positionwise scaling. On a small matched gender-agreement subset, positionwise norm matching leaves smaller observed mean gaps than full-output calibration. (3) Answer exclusion. Compared with unscaled NNLS, answer-excluded calibration reduces gaps in the measured subject-verb agreement comparisons but increases them for gender refits. Full-output KL calibration also reduces larger gaps for norm-matched constructed candidates, although matching coverage is incomplete in several settings. Since calibration uses the evaluated input's outputs, it serves as a diagnostic of residual disagreement.

papers.title: Propensity Straight-Through Gradients for Discrete Stochastic Systems
papers.summary: We introduce the propensity straight-through (PST) estimator for gradient-based learning through exact simulations of continuous-time Markov chains (CTMCs). These models describe discrete stochastic dynamics across physics, chemistry, and biology, but their categorical event choices prevent ordinary differentiation. PST preserves exact forward trajectories and differentiates, in the backward pass, the normalized reaction propensities the simulator already computes. The affine state update makes this rule exact for the one-step conditional-mean sensitivity. We derive the per-step discrepancy for one-step sensitivities composed along nonlinear trajectories in closed form, show that it vanishes for affine downstream dependence, and bound it quadratically in the stoichiometric jump size. Across reversible dimerization, a genetic oscillator, a 50-task repressilator suite, and experimental patch-clamp recordings, PST recovers parameters to within 0.06-1.7% and converges 2.4-3.0-fold faster than the Gumbel-Softmax straight-through estimator at matched computational cost. At deep-learning scale, PST trains all 203,796 parameters of a stochastic reaction network using exact discrete events from initialization. By differentiating an exact conditional mean, PST eliminates reaction-selection temperature tuning and provides a scalable route to learning through exact stochastic dynamics.

papers.title: Gaussian Approximation of Besov Functions for Logistic Classification on Manifolds
papers.summary: We study Gaussian kernel approximation and regularized logistic classification on a connected compact smooth embedded manifold $X\subset\mathbb R^d$ without boundary and of intrinsic dimension $\varrho$. Two main challenges are to derive a fast oracle inequality without assuming a bounded Bayes function and to construct Gaussian approximants that exploit both the intrinsic dimension and the target's regularity without saturation. We address the first challenge through a Bernstein-type inequality whose constant depends linearly on the supremum norm of the predictor. Combined with localized complexity estimates, this yields an oracle inequality over separable normed function spaces. To address the second challenge, we establish a uniform Sobolev operator expansion and cancel its lower-order bias terms using a signed combination of Gaussian kernel integral operators at different bandwidths. Real interpolation then gives an $L_2(X)$ approximation error of order $γ^α$ for functions in $B^α_{2,\infty}(X)$, where $γ$ is the bandwidth. By constructing the approximants directly on the manifold without ambient extension, we obtain a squared Gaussian RKHS norm bound of order $γ^{-\varrho}$. This construction thus overcomes second-order saturation while retaining norm control governed by the intrinsic dimension. When the marginal distribution has a density $g\in L_p(X)$, these results yield the logistic excess-risk rate $\bigl((\log n)^{\varrho+1}/n\bigr)^{4α(1-1/p)/(4α(1-1/p)+3\varrho)}$. We further show that clipping predictions yields the faster clipped logistic excess-risk rate $\bigl((\log n)^{\varrho+2}/n\bigr)^{2α(1-1/p)/(2α(1-1/p)+\varrho)}$. For bounded densities, its polynomial exponent matches that of the minimax optimal rate for squared-loss regression, and its corresponding excess misclassification risk also matches the minimax optimal rate.

papers.title: Quotient Geometry and Persistence-Stable Metrics for Swarm Configurations
papers.summary: Can temporal information recover geometry lost by a persistence diagram? For $n\ge3$ points on the unit sphere evolving under known homogeneous complete consensus, we prove generic local recovery modulo rotations and permutations from two ordinary zero-dimensional Vietoris--Rips persistence snapshots. The structural result applies to every labeled tree: its edge inner products and their first temporal derivatives have differential rank $2n-3$, exactly the dimension of the regular formation quotient. An explicit pole--equator witness proves this simultaneously for all tree types after taking a finite intersection of open dense sets. Although one snapshot has generic local fibers of dimension $n-2$, two sufficiently close snapshots are injective on a common neighborhood. The optimal inverse Lipschitz constant grows as $Θ(1/|h|)$ when the sampling interval tends to zero. A verified left inverse, interval derivative bounds, and explicit persistence-matching margins certify neighborhoods and time intervals at rational reference formations. The results are local and model-specific; reflection ambiguity and centered rank obstructions remain.
